SOFIA — The 6th China-Central and Eastern Europe High-Level Think Tank Scholars Forum, themed "China-Europe Dialogue: Expanding Synergies and Embracing a Win-Win Future," was held on Monday, bringing together more than 100 experts and scholars from Bulgaria, Croatia, Romania, Serbia and other countries.
Wang Junwei, director of the Academic and Editorial Committee of the Institute of Party History and Literature of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee, said in his keynote speech that seeking common ground while preserving differences and pursuing cooperation for mutual benefit are important principles guiding China's approach to international relations and valuable experience in ensuring the steady development of China-Europe relations. These principles will continue to play a guiding role in cooperation between China and Central and Eastern European countries (CEEC) in the future, he said.
In her welcome remarks, Chinese Ambassador to Bulgaria Dai Qingli said that as long as China and Europe uphold mutual respect and engage in equal-footed consultations, both sides will be able to find solutions to problems and continuously expand the scope for mutually beneficial cooperation.
Nataliya Kiselova, former president of the National Assembly of Bulgaria, said in her remarks that the fifth plenary session of the 20th Central Committee of the CPC demonstrated the CPC leadership's courage to uphold the truth and curb abuses of power, and its determination to continue consolidating its position as the core of leadership in Chinese society.
ALSO READ: China-CEEC cooperation opening doors
Wu Haitao, vice president of the China Public Diplomacy Association, said that think-tank exchanges serve as an important channel for continuously strengthening the public-opinion foundation of China-Europe friendship.
Participants held in-depth discussions on China's 15th Five-Year Plan, the four major global initiatives, global governance, and the prospects and vision for China-EU relations.
The inaugural forum was held in 2016. Since then, it has played an active role in facilitating exchanges of ideas and building consensus among think-tank scholars from China and CEEC.

This year's forum was jointly organized by the Scientific Research Planning Department of the Institute of Party History and Literature of the CPC Central Committee, the Chinese Embassy in Bulgaria, the China Public Diplomacy Association, the Bulgaria National Association for the Belt and Road, and Sofia University.

articles.title_orig: France Blames Iran for Cyberattack on Refrigeration Systems
articles.title_zh: France Blames Iran for Cyberattack on Refrigeration Systems
articles.content_orig:
France is "not ruling anything out" in its response to October's mass cyberattacks on supermarket refrigerators that the country has blamed on Iran, the country's Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said on Tuesday.
The French government summoned Iran's ambassador Tuesday morning after Paris said Monday that the findings of an investigation laid the blame for the hacks on Shahid Kaveh, an affiliate of the cyber unit of the powerful Revolutionary Guard Corps.
Barrot told radio station Franceinfo that the French government could respond with bans on entering European territory and the freezing of assets of anyone held responsible, as it looks to deter any further malicious acts conducted against the region.
Remote hacks on around 700 grocery stores over the night of Oct. 11 to Oct. 12 caused refrigerators and freezers to heat up by as much as 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit).
The soaring temperatures spoiled food and sparked fires, generating tens of millions of dollars in damage. Major French retailers, including Intermarché, E. Leclerc, Carrefour , Monoprix and Coopérative U were targeted.
The Paris Prosecutor's Office is seeking international arrest warrants, Paris chief prosecutor Laure Beccuau said in a statement.
Investigators found use of Farsi and IP addresses pointing to devices in Iran, according to the statement, which added that the attacks were committed to serve a foreign power, in this case, Iran.
The hacks targeted refrigeration controllers supplied by Danfoss and Dixell, with attackers remotely taking control of the equipment through web interfaces and starting unlimited defrost cycles while disabling the safety alerts on sensors designed to activate when temperatures exceed a set threshold, it said.
The French government also said Monday that it would propose new European sanctions against any Iranian entities and individuals involved, and summon the Iranian Ambassador.
"France condemns in the strongest possible terms the unacceptable cyberattacks carried out on its territory by the Islamic Republic of Iran against its interests," France's Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs said in a statement.
"This is an unprecedented campaign in terms of its scale and level of aggressiveness, thus constituting the first cyber offensive campaign carried out purely for the purpose of sabotage on national territory."
"This actor poses a persistent threat to our critical infrastructure. These destructive cyberattacks are unjustifiable, inexcusable, and violate international law," the ministry said.
CNBC has contacted the Iranian government for comment.
France attributes several previous cyberattacks on the country to Iran-based actors, including cyberattacks and "information manipulation campaigns" against the newspaper Charlie Hebdo in 2023 and the Paris Olympics in 2024. Those led to sanctions in March 2026 against private Iranian company Emennet Pasargad.
More supermarket fridges elsewhere in Europe were targeted in November, with stores across Belgium, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Finland, Ireland and Sweden reporting losses.
French blood banks were also affected on Nov. 2 by cybersecurity attacks, the French Blood Establishment said.
Temperature and defrost thresholds at cold storage units used to store blood products and samples headed to healthcare settings and biobanks were "set to excessively high levels," the EFS said in a statement translated from French to English by CNBC.
European leaders and the public have meanwhile been rattled by a wave of hoax bomb threats that have caused dozens of passenger flights to perform emergency landings.
"It feels like this could be a pretty unsubtle message from hostile actors to European governments warning that..[they] have the capability to interfere with critical infrastructure and disrupt essential services whenever they choose," Simon Edwards, CEO of cybersecurity testing lab SE Labs, said in an emailed comment.
"Whether this is an attempt to intimidate governments or preparation for something bigger, it shows how vulnerable our infrastructure can be."
"The lack of basic cybersecurity hygiene is the key factor making these attacks possible, why were these fridges connected to the internet in the first place, and accessible without passwords?"
— CNBC's Emma Graham and Sawdah Bhaimiya contributed to this story.

Sitting in the park with her grandchildren one afternoon, Becky Tucker decided to overhaul her life.
As the four of them played and ran around, Becky, then 48, simply lacked the energy to join in. It was, she says now, a wake-up call.
The risk management consultant from Poole, Dorset, had been struggling with fatigue, anxiety, mood swings and hot flushes as perimenopause took hold.
And for as long as she could remember, she had experienced intense, debilitating migraines for a week every month, linked to her menstrual cycle.
She was also significantly overweight – something she had struggled with her whole life. At more than 13 stone and with a BMI of 29 – bordering on obese – Becky had spent the previous 25 years on various weight-loss plans.
They'd worked, to begin with, but then she piled on the pounds again when she returned to her usual diet of chocolate bars and what she calls 'beige stodge'.
It will be a familiar scenario to many in midlife – the pounds creep on until it no longer feels possible to shift them.
But three years on, it is no exaggeration to say that Becky is transformed. Indeed, as our photos show so clearly, she is almost unrecognisable. Fizzing with energy and an astonishing four stone lighter, she says she feels like a different woman.
Becky Tucker shed four stone by following the ZOE diet. The risk management consultant from Poole, Dorset, had  previously struggled with fatigue, anxiety, mood swings and hot flushes

Her enviably slender figure has shrunk by more than four dress sizes, from a 16 to an 8 or 10. Her near-lifelong migraines have vanished, as have those limiting menopause symptoms.
And most importantly of all? She is now running around the park with her grandchildren, no longer stuck on a bench at the sidelines.
But what is extraordinary is that Becky achieved it – and she says this almost apologetically – 'without really trying'.
There was no restrictive diet, no calorie counting, and no pangs of hunger. My exclusive six-week ZOE diet plan will show you how to eat your way to better health, with delicious recipes, simple changes and no calorie counting.

Based on Professor Spector’s research at ZOE, and including recipes from his new cookbook Good Mood Food, the series will guide you, step-by-step, through a new way of eating that could transform not just your waistline, but most importantly how you feel every day.
You'll discover the surprisingly simple foods that nourish the trillions of bacteria living in your gut, why these microbes may hold the key to better mood and brain health, and how to feed them.
We'll show you what to put in your shopping basket – and what to leave on the shelves – and how to build delicious, filling meals.
There will be exclusive recipes, from hearty breakfasts and satisfying dinners to indulgent desserts, along with expert advice on eating to support your mood and thinking as you get older.
Halfway through, Professor Spector will make a live appearance on dailymail.com to answer readers' questions and talk about his cookbook.
And as Christmas approaches he'll reveal how to enjoy your favourite festive foods without undoing all your hard work – and, crucially, how to make these changes stick for life.
Indeed, research by Professor Spector's gut health company ZOE found that 35 per cent of around 5,000 participants lost at least 5 per cent of their body weight in just three months.
Their approach to diet has become a global phenomenon, refined through years of research involving hundreds of thousands of people.
Although more personalised recommendations are available to ZOE subscribers, anyone can follow the basic principles, for free.
Becky overhauled her diet with the help of nutrition science company ZOE, co-founded by Professor Tim Spector, the scientist at the forefront of discoveries in diet and gut health
These include eating 30 different plants a week, by making simple tweaks such as sprinkling seeds, nuts or fresh herbs over a salad or soup, or adding chopped fruit or greens to a plate.
Professor Spector encourages dieters to swap meat, particularly processed meat such as sausages, bacon and salami, for plant-based proteins including beans, lentils and chickpeas, and to aim for at least 30g of fibre a day.
However, chicken, lean meat and especially oily fish can still be enjoyed as part of his approach.
Ultra-processed foods, or UPFs – industrially-produced foods lacking in nutrients and containing cosmetic additives designed to make food irresistible to eat – are discouraged.
Instead, meals should be based on whole foods, with a rainbow of different-coloured plants to maximise nutrients.
'Studies have found that people who eat healthy diets, full of fruit, vegetables and whole grains, significantly improve their mood,' Professor Spector says.
'On the other hand, people who eat the most UPFs such as crisps, biscuits, sausages, sugary soft drinks, chicken nuggets and sugary cereal, have the biggest risk of mental health problems and dementia.
'When people have moderate depression, giving them a gut-friendly diet can improve or reverse symptoms in a significant proportion of them.'
Despite this, processed foods such as baked beans, Weetabix and high-fibre or seeded bread are on the menu.
Fermented foods, including natural yogurt, sourdough bread, kefir, sauerkraut, kombucha and kimchi, also have a role to play, as do dark chocolate and peanut butter. Most of these feature in the cookbook.
'It's not about restriction or cutting out all processed foods,' he explains, 'it's about cutting back on the worst unhealthy ultra-processed foods and replacing them with real whole plants'.
Eating more whole foods increases fibre intake – nine in ten Britons fail to get the recommended 30g a day, which can help protect against bowel cancer, cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes.
All ZOE studies to date have shown improvements in mood and energy within the first two weeks in the majority of people.
High-fibre foods also make you feel fuller for longer and can stimulate the release of GLP-1, the appetite-regulating hormone mimicked by weight-loss drugs.
Becky, now 52, is proof of how powerful these changes can be – with benefits she never expected.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang lobbied ‘very good friend’ Trump for more Nvidia sales to China while ‘caught in Beijing’s honeytrap’
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang lobbied ‘very good friend’ Trump for more Nvidia sales to China while ‘caught in Beijing’s honeytrap’
articles.content_orig:
SAN FRANCISCO — Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang made himself President Trump’s “very good friend” and lobbied the administration to loosen restrictions on AI chip sales to China while he was allegedly ensnared in a Chinese honeytrap, a timeline of his reported relationship with Alice Huang shows.
The $150 billion AI boss appeared in loved-up snaps with accused communist spy Alice Huang last year — and then weeks later personally pitched Trump at the White House on relaxing export restrictions for the company’s chips.
Huang missed Trump’s second inauguration, but then more than made up for it with a $25 million donation to the president’s ballroom project.
The 63-year-old appeared at a $1 million-per-person dinner at Mar-a-Lago in April 2025, where he pushed to lift chip restrictions that had just been imposed. There were at least three documented meetings between Trump and Huang where the administration responded with policy changes that made it easier for Nvidia to sell advanced chips to China.
China hawks have long pushed to restrict the most cutting edge chips from the communist regime in an attempt to blunt its technological advances and stymie its attempts to overtake the US on AI.
Huang, for his part, had lobbied and spoken out against restrictions since the Biden administration first imposed limits in 2022. Additionally, selling more chips to the world’s second largest economy could only help Nvidia’s bottom line.
But all the while, Huang — who has been married to college sweetheart Lori for more than 40 years — was meeting with 42-year-old Alice. In May 2025, they were spotted at dinner together during Taiwan’s top tech expo, where she looked at him adoringly and affectionately touched his arm as they sat with other tech honchos.
Alice Huang — a TV host, turned banker, turned executive at the Singapore-based AI computing company Megaspeed — met Jensen Huang (no relation) in early 2024, according to reports. Megaspeed has bought billions of dollars in chips from Nvidia for data centers in Southeast Asia and the Middle East.
Separately, the firm — backed by Chinese tech giant Alibaba — is under investigation for allegedly smuggling chips to China. The US government is probing reports that 50,000 chips sold to Megaspeed were seemingly missing following an audit.
Nvidia reportedly intervened in that probe, according to Bloomberg.
The Chinese government denies allegations of a honeypot spy scheme. Megaspeed also denies allegations of wrongdoing.
Trump himself has downplayed Huang’s admission of infidelity and Nvidia’s board said the company, which has no succession plan for replacing Huang, had full confidence in him, even as it announced it was investigating the claims.
On Monday, Trump said he called to check on Huang after he admitted cheating on his wife and apologized to his family.
“I did speak to him today just to see if he’s feeling all right,” Trump said at the White House. “He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy. I asked him that question. Did you have any idea that she was a spy? He said I had no idea that she was a spy, and I really believe him.”
The president and the Nvidia “have become good friends,” a source close to them told The Post.
Huang has made himself an integral part of the US economy. Nvidia reached a historic $5.5 trillion in valuation in May 2026, beating out Apple at the time as the most valuable public company in the entire world. It is both the world’s most important chipmaker, and the locus around which the AI boom spins. It uses the profits from its sales to help fund AI companies building out data centers, spurring further demand for its products.
By some accounts the AI boom is expected to account for up to 4% of all US economic activity this year, and Nvidia’s revenues alone up to 1%.
Trump personally hailed Nvidia’s latest quarter record sales of $96.2 billion in September, up 106% from last year.
Huang notably traveled with the president during his trip to China last May, with Trump even going as far as to personally invite the Nvidia boss to ride with him on Air Force One.
When Huang couldn’t make it to Washington DC in time for departure, he took his private plane to Alaska to join the president during his refueling stop in Anchorage.
Dressed in his signature black leather jacket and carrying only a backpack, Jensen boarded the presidential plane alone, without an entourage, pausing to speak with Trump’s son Eric, who was also on the trip, as he boarded.
Huang and his wife were seated at the head table with the president and first lady Melania Trump at the September state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping . Trump was personally involved in selecting the guest list for that dinner, a source familiar with the planning told The Post.
Along with the gains for his company, Huang’s relationship with Trump reportedly came with some perks of power.
Huang called the president when his invitation to the April state dinner for King Charles arrived without a plus one, according to a source. The billionaire CEO wanted to bring his wife to the dinner.
When White House staff told him there were no plus ones, he called Trump and made a personal appeal, getting Lori Huang on the list and bumping a senior administration official off of it to make room for her, multiple administration sources told The Post.
Huang has two grown children with his wife, Spencer and Madison, who both work in their father’s company.
The family has a $38 million home in San Francisco , with Nvidia spending nearly $4 million in fiscal 2026 on services for Huang that included home security, protection during personal travel, consulting and drivers, according to its May proxy filing.
Huang has remained close to Trump, literally, traveling to the Middle East for Trump’s visit to Saudi Arabia and United Arab Emirates in May 2025, then to London to join the president at Windsor Castle for a state dinner with King Charles that September.
Trump, at a meeting with then-British Prime Minister Keir Starmer during that visit, saw the CEO in the audience and teasingly told him: “You’re taking over the world Jensen. I don’t know what you’re doing here. I hope you’re right.”
He also had a prime seat at Trump’s side at the September 29th meeting on AI policy , alongside other technology executives. And the president awarded him the National Medal of Science last month.
Huang and Trump remained close friends despite the warning signs about the Nvidia boss’ relationship with Alice, which one tech company flagged to the Commerce Department last summer.
“The White House has known how suspicious Ms. Huang, and her corporate network, is since last summer,” a source familiar with the case told The Post. “And Jensen has repeatedly lied about his relationship with Ms. Huang.”
Culper Research also published a report titled “NVIDIA (NVDA): The China Problem” in May 2026, which specifically warned about the concerning rumors about Nvidia’s chief executive and Alice.
Alice had been under investigation since the Biden administration and believed to have been recruited as an asset for China’s feared Ministry of State Security.
The Commerce Department first flagged Alice following her sudden rise to the top of Megaspeed in 2023.
The concerns were troubling enough that Secretary of State Marco Rubio pushed back on letting Huang attend the China state dinner with Trump, the source added.
Little is known about the alleged spy’s private life, but before entering the world of finance, Alice had worked as a reporter for CCTV, the national broadcaster of the Chinese state, and Hunan TV, a regional broadcaster in central China, according to her LinkedIn biography.
Local reports claimed Alice is married to former Shanghai Hexi chairman Kang Wei — a former business partner, whose firm was fined $2.7M and censured by the Shanghai Stock Exchange.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

The return of Pickles has given investors hope that The Trade Desk can return to its former glory, but they may be getting ahead of themselves.
That said, the stock is trading for just 18 times earnings, near an all-time low set just last month. Given the pessimism built into the stock price, it wouldn't take much to send The Trade Desk higher -- as evidenced by its movement today.
We'll know more soon, as The Trade Desk is scheduled to report its Q3 results after the market close today.

While everyone watches the chip designers, one "backbone" company provides the critical technology that Nvidia and AMD literally cannot function without. We've detailed this under-the-radar player in our new AI Playbook.

articles.title_orig: Russia, Ukraine and US officials hold talks in Abu Dhabi
articles.title_zh: Russia, Ukraine and US officials hold talks in Abu Dhabi
articles.content_orig:
Negotiators from Moscow, Kyiv, and Washington are holding talks in Abu Dhabi aimed at ending the war in Ukraine, ⁠the Russian news ⁠agency RIA ⁠Novosti reported.
The meeting in the United Arab Emirates capital on Tuesday is the third round of talks there this year, following security consultations in January and February.
The US delegation is led by President Donald Trump’s envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who have spearheaded Washington’s mediation.
Russia’s delegation is headed by presidential aide Vladimir Medinsky, while Ukraine is being represented by a team led by Rustem Umerov, head of the Foreign Intelligence Service.
The three delegations last met in Geneva on February 18.
Ahead of the talks, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that recent gains on the battlefield had strengthened his country’s hand.
“Ukrainian forces are currently genuinely strengthening Ukraine’s negotiating position,” Zelenskyy said in his nightly video address on Monday. He said Russia was “suffering record losses”, a claim Moscow disputes, and urged Washington to persuade the Kremlin to end the war.
Zelenskyy said armed forces chief General Mykhailo Drapatyi had presented a report on Ukraine’s military positions that pointed to heavy recent Russian losses. Zelenskyy also said Kyiv’s long-range strikes on targets inside Russia, including oil facilities, were having an effect.
“We are responding to Russia’s war in a fully justified manner and demonstrating that this war must end,” he said. “Russia can do this. It can end its war. It is important that the United States convince Russia of precisely this.”
In Washington, DC, Trump told reporters that he saw a “very strong inclination” towards ending the war and that both sides were “tired of fighting”.
“We’re having a very good conversation about that in Abu Dhabi,” he said.
Trump had promised to end the war quickly when he took office in January 2025, but a settlement has remained elusive nearly five years after Russia launched a full-scale invasion of its neighbour in February 2022.
A US official, briefing reporters on condition of anonymity, said on Monday that both Moscow and Kyiv had privately shown some flexibility on Ukrainian territory occupied by Russia. Security guarantees for Ukraine would be a central topic, the official said, including the possibility of a defence commitment modelled on Article 5 of NATO’s founding treaty.
Both Ukraine and Russia have been adamant about territory .
Ukraine wants Russia pushed back to the original border between the two countries, while Russian President Vladimir Putin wants to obtain all of Ukraine’s Donbas region.
Russia occupies roughly 20 percent of Ukraine , including Crimea and parts of eastern Donbas. Moscow’s claims to the Ukrainian regions it has occupied have not been recognised by the international community, but Trump has previously urged Kyiv to cede territory for a deal to end the war.
The US official said any territorial agreement would most likely come at the end of the negotiations, once other issues, including a post-war security framework, had been settled.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, struck a cautious note, saying the process to end the war still has “a ways to go”.
“We’ll keep trying. And that’s what we’ve been trying to do the whole time, is try to be creative and find ways that we can help bring that conflict and that war to an end,” Rubio said.
European powers, including France, Germany and the European Commission, said they would send officials to the talks in Abu Dhabi, but Russia made it clear it did not want the Europeans to take part in negotiations.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said the talks would focus on security guarantees. European officials would not take part, he added, because the negotiations had been agreed to as a three-way format.
“What will take place in Abu Dhabi in the coming days is trilateral negotiations between Russia and Ukraine with US mediation,” Peskov said. “As for the presence of Europeans, you know that the Americans have their own channels of communication with Europeans, and Ukrainians with Europeans.”

articles.title_orig: China’s Trade Surplus Passes $1 Trillion at Record Pace
articles.title_zh: China’s Trade Surplus Passes $1 Trillion at Record Pace
articles.content_orig:
China’s trade surplus surged past $1 trillion in the first 10 months as a global race to build AI infrastructure buoyed sales of high-tech products and helped offset weak domestic demand, a dynamic likely to sharpen tensions with major trading partners.
The figures highlight Beijing’s growing reliance on overseas demand to support an economy hobbled by subdued consumption and a protracted property slump. But while the global AI investment boom is expected to keep demand for Chinese technology products strong into 2027, it risks deepening domestic imbalances and fueling trade frictions with partners including the European Union.
Exports rose sharply by 35.2% in October from the same month last year in US dollar terms, customs data showed on Tuesday, only a touch slower than the 36.3% surge in September, but ahead of economists’ forecast for an increase of 33.5%.
That helped lift China’s trade surplus to $1.04 trillion in the first 10 months, topping $1 trillion for a second consecutive year and reaching the milestone a month earlier than in 2025.
The swelling surplus could fuel further tensions with the European Union , where leaders have called for more trade curbs with China after reaching an agreement with Beijing to limit Chinese exports of hybrid vehicles to the bloc over the next few years. Because the measures have yet to take effect, factories are expected to bring forward shipments, bolstering exports in the near term.
China economy grows thanks to AI export boom but domestic slump remains a drag
China on Monday officially announced the extension of a trade truce with Washington due to expire on November 10 by two months, but said last week that expanding its purchases of US farm goods would hinge on the implementation of their agreed reciprocal tariff-reduction arrangement.
“The risk of additional tariffs and other trade barriers will remain elevated in 2027, particularly as Chinese manufacturers continue expanding their presence in overseas markets,” said Joe Peissel, lead macroeconomist at Trivium China.
Imports grew 41.6%, beating the median forecast for a 32% increase in the Reuters poll and accelerating from the 31% growth in September.
The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit will take place next week in the southern Chinese tech and innovation hub Shenzhen, where Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump are expected to meet for the third time so far this year.
One big worry for Beijing is that consumers remain reluctant to spend, constrained by a property market downturn that has battered household wealth and dented confidence in the economic outlook.
Sluggish demand at home has pushed Chinese automakers to seek sales in overseas markets. China’s car exports maintained a solid pace of growth in October, while domestic vehicle sales recorded a 12th straight month of declines, separate data released by an industry association showed.
Greater reliance on exports, however, leaves China’s economy increasingly exposed to any slowdown in global demand.
Much of the strength in exports this year has been fueled by a global push to expand AI infrastructure.
“The outlook for exports depends on how long the AI boom will last,” Macquarie analysts wrote. They expect China’s exports to accelerate further in the fourth quarter before starting to slow from the first quarter of 2027.

Business live – latest updates
Oil prices have fallen to the lowest level since late August while stock markets climbed higher, as markets reacted with relief to Donald Trump saying that the war on Iran is “effectively over” .
Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, fell nearly 3% to $89.66, the lowest since 31 August, on Tuesday morning, after the US president downplayed the need for military action against Iran “at this point”. The fall came after a near 6% drop on Monday on signs that the conflict might be nearing an end.
Europe’s benchmark Stoxx 600 index gained 0.9% to 662.54, hovering near a record high, which it had hit in early August on hopes for a peace deal in the Middle East.
Airline stocks rose amid hopes that easing tensions could lead to lower fuel costs, with Lufthansa 1.8% ahead and Air France-KLM up 1.2%.
In London, the FTSE 100 index climbed 45 points, or 0.4%, to 10,828. The oil companies BP and Shell were the biggest losers, down 1.7% and 1.5% respectively.
During a White House press conference, Trump said Israel and Gulf allies in the region were well protected from Iran and an escalation was not needed.
“At this point, taking the military action doesn’t seem to be a very necessary thing – but we’re locked and loaded, ready to go for any reason,” he told reporters during a briefing at the White House.
Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at the trading platform Capital.com, said: “Global markets are extending their recovery this morning after Wall Street recorded a strong session that was relatively broad-based, supported by a sharp decline in oil prices and renewed buying in technology stocks.”
However, the US Federal Reserve will want more evidence of slowing inflation, she said. The latest US inflation data for October will be released at 1.30pm GMT.
Hathorn added: “Ultimately, markets are benefiting from an improvement in the geopolitical outlook, but the underlying macroeconomic and corporate risks remain unresolved. articles.title_zh: Nvidia’s China Spy Fallout Deepens: Report Says Moonshot AI Accessed NVDA’s Advanced Chips Despite Export Controls
articles.content_orig:
By ANDREW JEHRING, CHIEF FOREIGN CORRESPONDENT and JOHN-PAUL FORD ROJAS, DEPUTY BUSINESS EDITOR
Published: 19:17 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 22:08 EST, 9 November 2026
The Chinese 'spy' accused of honey-trapping the boss of the world's biggest AI chip firm had bragged that she could secure his firm's technology despite a US export ban.
Alice Huang pitched a deal to Beijing investors to secure Nvidia's coveted graphics processing units (GPUs) last year.
Ms Huang said she had 'no problem securing GPUs', the Financial Times reported, even though Chinese firms are barred from obtaining them by the US.
She did not disclose her relationship with Nvidia's married chief executive Jensen Huang, who is no relation, during the investment pitch for a data centre project in Singapore .
Washington imposed strict limits on the US firm's exports to thwart attempts by Chinese president Xi Jinping to become the leading AI superpower by 2030.
Nvidia went into meltdown on Monday after Mr Huang admitted having an affair with Ms Huang months after she was declared a Chinese spy by US intelligence.
On Sunday, the 63-year-old said in a memo to staff: 'I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did.'
The company has commissioned an independent probe into the affair. It lost around £292billion of its value – or 9 per cent – in minutes on Monday, equal to the combined value of HSBC and Barclays. Its shares recovered, but it was still down by 4 per cent by the evening, making it worth around £3trillion.
Nvidia Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang is pictured at a party with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang in June 2024
Mr Huang admitted he was 'unfaithful' to his wife, Lori Huang, who he is pictured with her during a visit to the White House on September 24
Ms Huang apparently worked as a Chinese state TV reporter and had a stint in private equity before she formed Megaspeed International in 2023, according to unverified internet biographies.
Within a year the previously dormant firm became the largest buyer of Nvidia's chips in south-east Asia. Weeks before they started purchasing the chips she was seen drinking whisky with Taiwan-born American businessman Mr Huang in Taipei – the first known pictures of them together.
Megaspeed's imports topped £3.6billion as it opened facilities across south-east Asia and rented the firm's technology to the Chinese tech giant Alibaba.
The investments set off alarm bells in Washington and Ms Huang was placed under surveillance at the end of 2024. Earlier this year she was named as a spy in a US intelligence report.
However, Donald Trump – a close ally of Mr Huang – did nothing, the New York Times reported.
Theresa Fallon, director of the Centre for Russia Europe Asia Studies in Brussels, said: 'It is always amazing to see how so-called intelligent people fall for a Chinese honey-trap.'
Rush Doshi, an assistant security studies professor at Georgetown University in Washington, said: 'If the reporting is right, this is the most significant story in US-China policy in years.
'If the US knew Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with a Chinese spy and looked the other way, all while that spy ran a company backdooring US compute to China, it warrants a Congressional investigation.'
America restricted firms from exporting advanced Nvidia chips to China in 2022, but some smuggled them illegally over the border. Others legally set up businesses that buy large numbers of chips to build data centres in south-east Asia that serve Chinese firms.
Ms Huang apparently worked as a Chinese state TV reporter and had a stint in private equity before she formed Megaspeed International in 2023, according to unverified internet biographies
Mr Huang is pictured with President Donald Trump last month
Megaspeed, based in Singapore, appeared to be a middle man, buying Nvidia chips and providing computing power to Chinese firms operating outside the country. However, it was suspected of smuggling the tech into China.
Mr Huang lobbied Mr Trump to relax export laws on chips, and when a US delegation visited China last May he was initially left off the list due to concerns about his 'influence on the President's policy of only lightly regulating AI'.
Silicon Valley giants defended the tech tycoon last night. Shaun Maguire, a partner at Sequoia Capital, a tech investment firm, tweeted that Mr Huang was 'irreplaceable for America's AI leadership', adding: 'My guess is there was no bad intention.' SpaceX boss Elon Musk said: 'I agree.'
Wall Street hedge fund manager Bill Ackman said: 'Jensen Huang is human. And he is an incredible human... even incredible humans make mistakes.'
China denied Ms Huang was a spy and accused the US of 'groundless smears and slanders'.
Nvidia said it 'prioritises US national and economic security' but 'has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.
It added that Mr Huang was co-operating with its investigation and would remain as chief executive pending the review.

articles.title_orig: European diplomats press Rubio for a role in Russia-Ukraine talks
articles.title_zh: European diplomats press Rubio for a role in Russia-Ukraine talks
articles.content_orig:
European foreign ministers have told United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio that Europe must have a say in any deal to end Russia’s war on Ukraine, as US-mediated peace talks get under way in Abu Dhabi.
They made the appeal on Monday in Paris, at a meeting of foreign ministers from the Group of Seven, which includes Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States.
It was Rubio’s first meeting with allies since last week’s midterm elections, in which President Donald Trump’s Republican Party suffered stunning losses. The meeting gave Washington’s allies a chance to air their concerns with Rubio directly amid concern about Trump’s growing rhetoric of a new security architecture for Europe.
“It is certainly neither necessary, nor right, nor appropriate to make a fundamental change” to Europe’s security architecture, said German Minister for Foreign Affairs Johann Wadephul after talks with Rubio.
“Europe belongs at this table. There can be no solution without Europe – only with Europe,” he added.
The two-day Paris meeting, which ends on Tuesday, overlaps with the talks between Russia and Ukraine, scheduled for Tuesday and Wednesday.
Wadephul said the Abu Dhabi talks must show whether Russia is “genuinely prepared to negotiate”, urging Moscow to “give up maximalist demands” and warning against any “negotiation show” in the capital of the United Arab Emirates.
With Russian attacks on Ukraine’s civilian infrastructure continuing, he said, “we see no substantial contribution whatsoever toward negotiations gaining any serious momentum” from Moscow.
Andrii Sybiha, Ukraine’s foreign minister, is set to join a session on Ukraine in Paris on Tuesday.
“No one has the right to decide our fate behind our backs,” Sybiha said before departing for the meeting.
The Paris meeting comes as G7 members have grown increasingly uneasy with the direction of US policy, including Washington’s scaling back of support for Ukraine and of sanctions on Russia, as well as its increasingly unilateral course.
Ministers from Saudi Arabia, Egypt, South Korea and Brazil are also attending.
Iran is expected to feature prominently in the discussions on Tuesday.
Washington’s G7 allies have repeatedly voiced scepticism about the US and Israeli war on Iran and fear that further US military action could deepen the crisis rather than resolve it.
Al Jazeera’s Rebecca Collard, reporting from Paris, said the first day of talks had wrapped up with little clarity on US policy after the midterm elections.
“The second day of talks will include a session on instability in the Middle East,” she said.
“But there is something bigger up for discussion, too: The future of the multilateralism that has dominated relations among these countries for decades.”

articles.title_orig: Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy
articles.title_zh: Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy
articles.content_orig:
US President Donald Trump has said the FBI is investigating the affair between the chief executive of Nvidia and an alleged Chinese spy.
Trump said he spoke to Jensen Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign.
"I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters.
Beijing has rejected claims that Huang was targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".
Speaking later at a White House press briefing, Trump told reporters, "I know the FBI is looking into" the affair but did not give further details on the investigation, or confirm when it was launched.
Trump added he thought that Huang was an "honourable guy and I feel very confident that he will be in good shape" after the investigations.
The FBI declined to comment when contacted by the BBC.
Nvidia, which has commissioned an independent investigation into the affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy, said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised.
Nvidia is the world's second most valuable company after Apple, and designs computer chips that have become central to AI technology.
The revelations knocked about $250bn (£190bn) off Nvidia's value on Monday as the company's share price fell by more than 4%.
US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang , also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report. She is not related to Jensen Huang.
According to the newspaper, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington in spring this year, warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.
Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia.
Trump's remarks are the first indication of whether Nvidia's Huang knew about the woman's alleged ties to Chinese espionage.
Megaspeed's office in Singapore's central business district appeared to be operational and staffed on Tuesday.
The BBC was refused entry to its floor, but spoke to a staff member by phone who said they had no comment and directed all queries to the company's PR team.
The BBC has emailed Megaspeed several times for comment.
Nvidia, co-founded by Jensen Huang, is also a major focus in the AI technology race between the US and China, with officials in Washington treating its exports to Beijing as a matter of national security - a key reason why Huang's affair has sparked concerns.
Also on Monday, Huang and Nvidia were sued in a proposed class action lawsuit in California that accuses them of defrauding shareholders by concealing his ties with the suspected Chinese spy.
The lawsuit alleges that the company lied to the media about Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, "who is suspected of seeking to help smuggle Nvidia products to China."
The BBC has contacted Nvidia for comment on the lawsuit.
At the White House, Trump was asked several times when he was made aware of the relationship. He said he was informed "over a period of time" but was not specific.
"I hope there's no problem, I believe he is suffering greatly," the president added.
He said he spoke to Huang on the phone on Monday "just to see if he's feeling alright, how you doing and I asked him about that and he said he absolutely had no idea that the person in question was a spy".
Trump has raised concerns that allowing China to lead in AI would supercharge Beijing's military and surveillance capabilities.
The president added he was "sure" Chinese leader Xi Jinping would "ask me about it" when they next met.
Huang has admitted that he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children.
He said on Monday that he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation the company had launched.
Huang has also been requested to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees next week, however it is unclear whether Huang will appear.
A letter said the briefing would be "on Nvidia's security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and your interactions with a publicly reported People's Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset: Megaspeed executive Alice Huang".
Nvidia has declined to comment, while the the BBC has also contacted the committees.
Some workers the BBC spoke to at Nvidia's Santa Clara headquarters on Monday said it was business as usual, despite the intense attention on the company.
Nvidia has been around for decades, with Huang founding it with two other engineers in 1993, but its rise to one of the world's most valuable and powerful companies has only been recent.
It originally designed computer chips for gaming, but its decision to shift focus to AI development turned it into the powerhouse it is today.
Its chips have become so valuable to the AI buildout that the White House previously imposed controls on where its advanced products could be sold.
The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US.
But Huang has long been against restricting sales to China, arguing that it would be better for the global rollout of AI to be powered by US technology.
In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions.
Nvidia's most advanced AI semiconductors including the GB200 Blackwell super chip remain blocked from the Chinese market.

articles.title_zh: Hungary detains Viktor Orban's brother in people-smuggling probe, PM says
articles.content_orig:
Arrest made by anti-corruption body set up to investigate alleged graft during former PM’s 16-year rule
Hungarian authorities have detained the brother of Viktor Orbán as part of a people-smuggling ⁠investigation, the prime minister, Péter Magyar , has said.
The Hungarian anti-graft body, the national asset protection and recovery office (NVVH), said in ⁠a statement it and ⁠police had ​detained four people and searched homes in Budapest and Pest county.
“Three ex-ministers of Orbán are already in custody,” Magyar said in Berlin, where he was giving a speech. “Already his brother today ⁠went to custody,” he added, referring to the former prime minister’s sibling, Aron, ​49.
Writing on Facebook, Orbán dismissed ‌his brother’s detention as a case of political revenge. “In this dirty game, the aim is the elimination of ‌the political opponent and the establishment of a one-party system. I am the target, my younger brother is just a tool,” the former prime minister wrote.
The NVVH ‌was set up by Magyar to investigate allegations of corruption during Orbán’s 16-year rule. The latter has denied the claims.
Magyar ​ousted Orbán in an April election and the NVVH is central to his government’s anti-graft campaign which he has dubbed “Operation Purgatory”.
Monday’s statement had said the four detained were suspected of helping Vietnamese citizens reach western Europe for several months in 2024.

The Japanese investment giant also recorded a 597.2 billion ($3.7 billion) yen loss in the six months ending on Sept. 30 due to changes in procurement plans for power generation equipment for AI data center projects in the U.S.
SoftBank said it had made advance investments to secure power generation equipment for its AI data center projects in the U.S. amid concerns over potential shortages and long procurement lead times. Power is increasingly becoming a key constraint for the AI data center buildout as power grids become overwhelmed with applications from large energy users like data centers.
Cumulative payments for power-generation equipment for U.S. AI data center projects, like the PORTS-Pike Technology Campus in Pike County, Ohio, totaled $9.48 billion as of the end of September.
"We made bridge investments in advance to secure power generation equipment in anticipation of shortage," a SoftBank executive said during the company's earnings call.

Revenue rose 13.3% in the six months ended Sept. 30, supported by growth in telecommunications and AI computing businesses. The company said its SoftBank segment recorded higher sales across all businesses, while revenue at its AI computing segment increased.
The company's Vision Fund segment swung to a loss of 81.58 billion yen in the fiscal second quarter, compared with a profit of 2.38 trillion yen a year earlier. Vision Fund 1 recorded an investment loss of $20 million in the quarter, despite a $1.3 billion gain on ByteDance, as shares of publicly traded portfolio companies, including Coupang and Grab, declined.
The Vision Funds segment recorded investment gains of 85.45 billion yen, down sharply from 2.81 trillion yen in the year-earlier period. Vision Fund 2 posted investment gains of 89.26 billion yen, while Vision Fund 1 recorded a loss of 3.86 billion yen on its investments.
As of the end of September, SoftBank's cumulative investment in OpenAI stood at $54.6 billion, with a fair value of $99.6 billion and a cumulative investment gain of $45 billion, according to the company.
SoftBank said a potential increase in OpenAI's valuation following a new funding round had not yet been reflected in its results, pending an official announcement. The updated valuation could be reflected in the fiscal third quarter, potentially boosting its net asset value and improving its loan-to-value ratio, the company said.
"ChatGPT has been continuously a weapon of OpenAI, especially for consumers," the SoftBank esecutive said during the company's earnings call, highlighting the chatbot's growing user base.
Shares of the Japanese investment giant closed 13.9% higher on Tuesday. The gains came as Asian technology stocks, including Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, rose following an overnight rebound on Wall Street.
On its AI infrastructure investments, SoftBank highlighted a 20-year lease agreement with OpenAI for eight gigawatts of IT capacity at a data center project in Ohio.
Addressing concerns of water consumption at its planned data center in Texas, SoftBank said it was taking steps to reduce water use through a closed-loop, air-cooled system. The company also pointed to plans to hire and source locally.
Ahead of its earnings release, SoftBank Group announced on Monday plans with Grab and Malaysia's PETROS to commit a combined $1.85 billion in initial capital to develop AI infrastructure in Malaysia, with a long-term target of at least five gigawatts of AI computing capacity.

articles.title_zh: Google Issues Chrome Security Update for Eighth Actively Exploited Zero-Day of 2026
articles.content_orig:
Google on Monday released updates to patch nine security vulnerabilities, including one that has come under active exploitation in the wild.
The high-severity vulnerability, assigned the CVE identifier CVE-2026-125350 (CVSS score: N/A), has been described as a use-after-free bug in the XML component.
Use-after-free bugs typically occur when a program attempts to access a memory location after it has already been freed. Successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to achieve data corruption, program crashes, or arbitrary code execution.
An anonymous security researcher has been credited with discovering and reporting the flaw on November 6, 2026.
Google acknowledged it is "aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-125350 exists in the wild," but has not revealed any additional specific information related to how it's being abused in real-world attacks or who is behind them.
"Access to bug details and links may be kept restricted until a majority of users are updated with a fix," the tech giant added. "We will also retain restrictions if the bug exists in a third-party library that other projects similarly depend on, but haven't yet fixed."
With the latest development, Google has addressed a total of eight actively exploited Chrome zero-days since the start of the year. This includes CVE-2026-2441, CVE-2026-3909, CVE-2026-3910, CVE-2026-5281, CVE-2026-11645, CVE-2026-85046, and CVE-2026-87491.
For optimal protection, users are advised to update their Chrome browser to versions 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and Apple macOS, and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux. To ensure the latest updates are installed, users can navigate to More > Help > About Google Chrome and select Relaunch.
Users of other Chromium-based browsers, such as Microsoft Edge, Brave, Opera, and Vivaldi, are also advised to apply the fixes as and when they become available.

'We support the work of those who are trying to limit the harm generative AI is doing to videogames and our world, and apologise that Big Walk’s LLM usage may not meet their standards'
When a number of IGF jurors took a hard stance on AI-developed video games yesterday we wrote a fairly standard blog about the news , but not long after the story was first published some additional, and deeply divisive, discussions emerged concerning one of the best video games of the year.
While the IGF jurors did not name any games in particular when outlining their opposition, it only took a few hours for news to emerge across social media that one of (if not the) biggest contributors to the "fairly intense discussion and disagreement across the judge and jury pools" was the revelation that Big Walk had used AI "in the final stretch" of the game's development.
Developers House House tell Aftermath "LLMs were used sparingly by House House to help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs", and that they "estimate that well under 0.1% of Big Walk’s code had anything to do with this usage". They also stress that "generative AI was not used in any other context when making the game".
House House also say they understand opposition to the news, adding "We have some concern that voluntary disclosures like this might contribute to the normalisation of this technology, or its treatment as 'inevitable'. We support the work of those who are trying to limit the harm generative AI is doing to videogames and our world, and apologise that Big Walk’s LLM usage may not meet their standards."
Despite this seemingly minor use of AI, the fact remains the game used AI in development, which for some in the IGF jury pool (and beyond) was clearly a huge disappointment, especially given the game's other progressive stances . For others, however, it's merely a sign of the times, or an instance where people's distrust and exhaustion with the tech was causing them to alienate a game that otherwise had been among many's shortlist for GOTY.
As for why House House is only confirming AI use in the game now, rather than at release, they say "We have not made any disclosure on Steam as the platform does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage. We are posting this disclosure as it has become a matter of public interest."
For future games, the studio says "Big Walk was developed without an internal AI usage policy in place, and we consider that lack of policy a failure. We will work to have a more comprehensive policy going forwards."

articles.title_zh: Anthropic Filing Snafu Jolts Investors in Run-Up to Mega IPO
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic's upcoming initial public offering could be a crucial test of investor confidence in the artificial intelligence trade, CNBC's Jim Cramer said on Monday.
"Without it, I don't see how the AI-related stocks can make a real recovery," the " Mad Money " host said, exactly two weeks after the Claude developer filed its S-1 IPO paperwork. Despite the recent sell-off in AI stocks, Anthropic is reportedly moving ahead with its IPO plans. The company is expected to meet with major investors this week and is targeting a trading debut as early as Thursday or Friday of next week, the Wall Street Journal reported , citing people familiar with the matter. "I don't think it's hyperbolic to say that this could be one of the most consequential IPOs in history."
Cramer explained that the billions of dollars being spent on AI chips and data centers ultimately depend on a handful of AI developers, including Anthropic, generating enough revenue to justify those investments.
"Anthropic is important because it is one of just a few companies at the end of the food chain for all of the AI data center investments that we've seen, so it is one of the few companies that, ultimately, needs to make money from all of this investment spending," Cramer said. "If it can't do that, or if it cannot convince enough investors that it will do so, then it's tough to justify all of the AI investments that are being made today."
Cramer pointed to SpaceX as an example of how interconnected the AI trade has become. Much of the Elon Musk rocket and AI company's recent revenue growth has come from renting computing capacity to customers, including Alphabet's Google and Anthropic. Google pays roughly $900 million a month for that capacity, while Anthropic's commitment has grown from an initial $1.25 billion monthly to more than $3 billion, according to its IPO prospectus.
Those contracts allow for SpaceX's massive purchases of Nvidia chips. "But if an Anthropic deal fails?" Cramer said. "Then Anthropic wouldn't have the cash to fulfill its contracts, and you'd have to take down estimates for both SpaceX and Nvidia, along with a whole host of other compute providers to Anthropic, and their suppliers." Not to mention, Alphabet, Amazon , and Nvidia have all invested in Anthropic, making their earnings sensitive to changes in the AI developer's valuation.
The wrinkle here is that investor appetite for an Anthropic IPO appears to be weakening. Anthropic's potential valuation has reportedly fallen from as much as $2 trillion earlier this fall to as low as $1 trillion following last week's technology sell-off on concerns that the Democratic wave in the midterm election will mean slower new data center construction.
On Friday, during the CNBC Investing Club's Annual Meeting , Cramer also stressed the importance of the Anthropic offering to the AI trade and to Club portfolio names Alphabet, Amazon and Nvidia.

The Food and Drug Administration on Monday warned that GLP-1 drugs carry a potential risk for a rare but serious eye condition and required pharma companies to inform patients and doctors of the risk.
The condition, called non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, or NAION, is sometimes referred to as an “eye stroke” and is caused by insufficient blood flow to the optic nerve. It typically causes sudden vision loss and, in severe cases, can lead to blindness. There are currently no proven treatments for the condition.
GLP-1 drugs such as Novo Nordisk’s Ozempic and Wegovy and Eli Lilly’s Mounjaro and Zepbound have exploded in popularity for their potent weight loss effects, but as with any drugs that are given to large populations, side effects can show up in real-world use that weren’t observed in clinical trials.

articles.title_orig: Faisal Islam: What the boss of US tech giant Nvidia told me about China and national security
articles.title_zh: Faisal Islam: What the boss of US tech giant Nvidia told me about China and national security
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang has the air of the late Steve Jobs about him. I have interviewed both, and the up-close charisma - and occasionally scratchy genius - is shared.
Both sported a signature item of black clothing, although Huang opts for a leather jacket rather than the Apple founder's turtle neck.
Both are innovators revered in the tech world.  However, Huang is now being investigated over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy .
Everything you have heard about Artificial Intelligence (AI) over the past few months - good, bad, revolutionary and catastrophic - is dependent on having the most powerful frontier AI models.
In turn they depend on the most powerful microchips, and for years that has been this very company, Nvidia, led by Huang, and his technology rooted in repurposed games graphics and the manufacturing prowess of Taiwan.
Names such as Gracehopper, Vera and Rubin mean almost nothing to the public, but are the names of chips powering the creation of AI models transforming the world.
I met Huang as he held court with reporters and offered words of encouragement for the UK's tech future during US President Donald Trump's state visit to the UK in September last year.
It was also right in the middle of his attempts to get Trump to lift export bans to China of some of the highest performing AI chips, specifically the H200.
An export ban on a less powerful chip had already been lifted. He was, I suggested to him, one of the few people who could walk into the White House to meet Trump, and a few days later meet President Xi Jinping in Beijing.
He made no secret of his views, nor his assessment that he had persuaded Trump of his case.
"President Trump is very clear. He wants America to win and and President Xi wants China to win, and it's possible for both of them too. And the reason for that is because it's not a zero-sum game. The advance of human society is not a zero-sum game."
He is probably the only person in the world that could have spoken that sentence with the authority that he might have heard personally from both these superpower leaders.
However, his view about "zero-sum game" is not backed by many in national security circles.
Their view is that the race to the most advanced forms of AI is entirely zero sum, and requires the West - and the US in particular - to take critical action to hold back Chinese advancement.
The country that creates the most powerful AI systems, from the most powerful chips, will win, in terms of scientific development, of cracking encryption, economic growth and cyber-weapons.
He made a further argument: Far from being a national security challenge, it was, in fact, better for the US that the world "including China" became dependent on US systems, what they called the "American tech stack", with Nvidia chips at its core.
Huang then went even further than that, saying that President Trump "is very clear-eyed" about the idea that "this computing technology is not a national security concern".
He told me "any military is smart enough to build their military on top of their own indigenous technology, and not rely on an adversary to build their technology, build their military capability".
At that time, which is the same moment now being independently investigated over national security concerns and alleged Chinese espionage, Huang was making clear public arguments to lift export bans, and seemed to have a clear idea of President Trump's views.
More than that, he was also disputing the idea that his technology, in China's hands, was any type of national security concern.
Nvidia is the absolute epicentre of the AI tech boom in the US and of the global race for AI supremacy.
Even if the boom turned to bust, Nvidia is still expected to remain in rude health.
It has actual hard revenues of about $400bn this year. Monday's drop of about 4% of its value reflects new and extraordinary risks at this junction of tech and global politics, but the chipmaker is still worth more than $4 trillion.

articles.title_orig: ‘Like gods reigning over humans’: Many defectors see daughter of North Korea's Kim as heir apparent
articles.title_zh: ‘Like gods reigning over humans’: Many defectors see daughter of North Korea's Kim as heir apparent
articles.content_orig:
Until she fled North Korea three years ago , Kim Yumi felt deeply frustrated whenever state TV showed leader Kim Jong Un with his young daughter.
The message, she felt, was clear and worrying: North Korea was laying the groundwork for an eventual hereditary transfer of power, this time to Kim’s daughter .
Publicly questioning the Kim dynasty’s hold on power would mean severe persecution. Already angered by draconian pandemic regulations that ruined her family’s fishing business, she defected to South Korea by boat with her family.
“My husband and I didn’t want our children to live under a fourth-generation dictatorship. As parents, we thought the best thing we could do for our children was to give them freedom,” said Kim Yumi, 32, who now lives in Seoul.
North Korea allows no dissent and harshly punishes attempts to flee the country. Established in 1948, the nation is nominally a socialist republic, but in reality it is an authoritarian dynasty , with three generations of the Kim family ruling in succession.
There was no known public resistance during its previous two successions — from state founder Kim Il Sung to his son Kim Jong Il in 1994 and then from Kim Jong Il to his son Kim Jong Un in 2011.
This time, North Korea is apparently trying something radical.
Kim Jong Un’s repeated public appearances with his daughter over the past four years have led to speculation that she’s being groomed as her father’s heir.
The question of who will become North Korea’s next leader is crucial because that person will face a huge challenge — governing an impoverished, nuclear-armed nation whose 26 million people have little political freedom and live under strict state surveillance while being cut off from much of the outside world.
North Koreans have no say in the selection of their future leader, and analysts and defectors say they will passively accept a third dynastic succession — at least publicly.
To gauge North Koreans’ private views, The Associated Press spoke with nearly a dozen defectors who still have contacts in North Korea or witnessed the country’s previous power successions, as well as several experts.
Not much is known about Kim’s daughter except that she’s reportedly about 13 and named Kim Ju Ae.
Since late 2022, she has made dozens of public appearances, all of them with her father at big events like weapons tests and military parades. State media has called her Kim’s “most beloved” and “respected” child. Her status has been emphasized by images showing an elderly general kneeling before her and her standing in front of her father.
South Korea’s spy agency says she is Kim’s likely heir. Eight of the 11 defectors interviewed by the AP shared that view; the others disagreed, citing the North’s deeply patriarchal culture.
“During her visits to missile launch sites and factories, the way senior North Korean officials treat Kim Ju Ae involves protocols reserved for a successor, not the ones simply for a daughter of Kim Jong Un,” said Tae Yongho, a former minister at North Korea’s Embassy in London who defected to South Korea in 2016. “They are repeating the same protocol and treatment they provided for Kim Jong Un,” when he accompanied his father as his heir.
Kang Mi-Jin, a defector who runs a company analyzing North Korea’s economy, said her contacts inside the North told her over smuggled phones that they think Kim Ju Ae is in line to succeed her father.
Jung Gwang-il, a defector who specializes in smuggling outside information to North Korea, said the North Koreans he meets as they visit Chinese border towns also hold the same belief.
Former NBA star Dennis Rodman was the first to reveal her identity, holding her as a baby during a 2013 trip to Pyongyang.
Much of the skepticism about Kim Ju Ae as a potential leader stems from her being female. South Korean officials believe she has a younger sibling whose gender hasn’t been confirmed.
Women in North Korea remain deeply underrepresented in senior posts. Only one of 17 department directors for the ruling Workers’ Party is a woman. That woman is Kim Jong Un’s influential younger sister, Kim Yo Jong, according to South Korea’s Unification Ministry.
“My contacts in North Korea say it would be nonsensical to revere that little girl as their supreme leader,” said Kim Jeong-Ah, a former North Korean army officer who resettled in South Korea in 2009.
Lee Si-young, a defector who heads the Seoul-based Free North Korea Radio station, said that some of her older contacts in North Korea aren’t happy with a woman taking power. But she said members of the Kim family “are like gods reigning over humans so gender really doesn’t matter.”
Whether or not the girl succeeds her father, observers agree that Kim Jong Un, 42, is likely to designate one of his children to prolong his family’s rule, a move they expect would face little resistance at home. South Korea’s spy agency recently assessed that Kim is extremely obese and at high risk of cardiovascular disease but shows no other signs of poor health.

North Koreans will passively “accept a hereditary succession as something that they should go along with,” said Ahn Chan-il, a defector and scholar who heads the World Institute for North Korean Studies in Seoul.
During North Korea’s first leadership transition, in 1994, the new leader, Kim Jong Il, then 52, had already spent two decades as the official successor working alongside his father to run the country.
The second succession, in 2011, was more uncertain. Kim Jong Un, who was then 27, was seen by outsiders as too young and inexperienced. He quickly consolidated his grip on power, however, by orchestrating high-profile executions and purges, including the 2013 killing of his powerful uncle Jang Song Thaek.
“A hereditary power succession system has been institutionalized in North Korea, just like presidential elections in our system,” said Oh Gyeong-seob, an analyst at Seoul’s Korea Institute for National Unification. “North Korea’s ruling elite accepts it as a matter of course. So do its general citizens.”
Choi Song-juk, who fled North Korea in 2015, said she had been so brainwashed that she had no complaints about the North’s two earlier power successions. She now calls them “nonsense.”
Defector Jeon Jae-hyun said North Korea’s pervasive surveillance apparatus keeps people from voicing their discontent with the government and helps enforce political loyalty.
Defector Kim Yumi said she had never heard about the girl until Kim Jong Un publicly introduced his daughter at a long-range missile launch site in November 2022.
“Ordinary people know absolutely nothing about private lives of the Kim family,” said Kim Yumi, who now runs a YouTube channel on North Korea. “They don’t really try to know about it and don’t pay attention to it because doing so could put them in danger.”

articles.content_orig:
For most businesses, an S-1 filing is fairly straightforward—a combination of due-diligence box-checking exercise and sales pitch. The registration statement is filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission ahead of an Initial Public Offering, or IPO, launch that allows the company to sell shares to the public for the first time. But the artificial intelligence industry seems poised to upend this rather dry business procedure, as demonstrated in Anthropic’s mammoth 400-page S-1 filed on October 26.
While the valuation for the AI company’s public offering (reportedly scheduled for November 16) is still confidential, estimates put it between $1.5 and $2 trillion, one of the largest IPO valuations ever and one which, as Trinity College professor Patrick Boyle pointed out, is roughly the size of Canada’s GDP .
There are several eye-catching figures buried in Anthropic’s S-1, to say nothing of the repeated mention of the possible existential risks Anthropic is worried it could usher in to the world. The company reported a 1,300 percent jump in revenue from a year ago, but also a net loss of $80.7 billion for the first half of 2026. As the Wall Street Journal noted, the company is also on the hook for $475 billion in compute capacity (read: data center) agreements over the next decade, the majority of which are noncancelable.
The scale of these finances is enormous, but they don’t only affect Anthropic. Should the company disappoint in its IPO launch, or fail to match its astronomical valuations, investor confidence in AI could be significantly shaken. That’s a problem when AI stocks have accounted for nearly three quarters of the S&P 500’s gains this year.
If Anthropic has any hopes of long-term sustainability, it needs to transform the hype around its product into paying customers to help offset the company’s massive costs. Ideally, those customers would be enterprise clients who can afford its significant fees. Currently, two enterprise clients (widely believed to be SpaceX and Microsoft) account for approximately one-fifth of Anthropic’s revenue.
To get there, the company has chosen to treat individual consumers as what its S-1 calls a “powerful top-of-funnel engine”: people who use Claude on their own and then push for its adoption at work. “We have consistently seen that individuals who experience Claude’s value firsthand become advocates within their organizations,” Anthropic’s S-1 reads . “They seed adoption that accelerates from individual use to team-wide and ultimately organization-wide deployment.”
The strategy is not new. As my colleague Ralph Bunche has noted in an analysis for NYU’s Stern Center for Business and Human Rights , where I work, Dropbox, Slack, and Zoom all pitched their free tiers as feeders for enterprise sales in their own S-1s. Bunche also notes that Anthropic was likely thinking about this shift as early as 2024, when it hired Instagram co-founder Mike Krieger as its chief product officer.
But while individual users are seen as key to Anthropic’s long-term viability , the company also admits that its product, when used regularly, could have effects on “mental health, cognitive development, and social behavior [which] are not yet fully understood.” Numerous cases have already highlighted the risks that AI systems pose to individual users, from sending them into hyperpersonalized delusional spirals to convincing them to take (incorrect and fatal) medical advice to allowing them to “ cognitively offload ” crucial critical-thinking skills. The S-1 further mentions that “risks relating to child safety may be particularly acute, as minors may be more susceptible to harmful content” and that “emergent capabilities may not be discovered until after a model has been deployed, potentially resulting in safety incidents … or the need to withdraw, retrain, or modify deployed models at significant expense.”
In Anthropic’s defense, the company has invested significant resources in attempting to design its AI in a safe and responsible manner, as befits a public benefit corporation. The S-1 notes how the company is required to balance the interests of its stockholders with “the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity.” Another relative rarity in Anthropic’s governance structure is the creation of a Long-Term Benefit Trust, or LTBT, which gives five financially disinterested trustees the power to elect and remove the majority of the board if necessary. Financial Times columnist Robert Armstrong likens this to a constitutional separation of powers, a structure that contrasts sharply with other AI companies, such as Meta, where Mark Zuckerberg controls 60.4 percent of the company’s voting power —despite holding only 13.4 percent of its economic ownership.
Finally, Anthropic’s Claude has shown itself to be a more responsible AI than its counterparts. In a March 2026 report by the Center for Countering Digital Hate , for instance, out of ten chatbots, Claude was one of two that consistently refused to assist users in planning violent attacks, and the only one that attempted to actively dissuade would-be attackers.
It’s fair to say, then, that Anthropic is actively trying to mitigate the risks from its product. But the company also admits (in a rather piecemeal manner) that its safeguards have limits. Its much-vaunted LTBT is not expected to intervene in the day-to-day running of the company. Meanwhile, the S-1 admits that safety measures “could slow our capability gains relative to competitors,” potentially putting it at a disadvantage. The end result is a company trying to emphasize safety while simultaneously positioning its regular consumers as both a key part of its sales strategy and test subjects in a massive public health experiment, the results of which the company doesn’t yet know.
This push-pull isn’t unique to Anthropic. It’s a struggle that every AI company is facing right now as it tries to balance safety against its business prospects and the need to engage new users. In August 2025, Reuters reported that Meta allowed its AI chatbots to “engage a child in conversations that [were] romantic and sexual.” Senator Josh Hawley subsequently opened an investigation into the company. In February, OpenAI researcher Zoë Hitzig quit over the company’s introduction of ads into its free tier, alleging that the company risked replicating the social media model of optimizing for engagement.
The industry’s pivot toward AI agents raises the stakes even further, as agents act over longer time horizons to carry out tasks on a user’s behalf. Meta’s Muse is a good example. While the agent topped the Apple App Store within days of its launch in September, there were also reports of it acting outside its parameters. In one case , Muse reportedly accepted a low offer for a listing on Facebook Marketplace and then shared the user’s home address with the buyer—all without telling him. Separately, Axios reported earlier in October that major U.S. banks were detecting unauthorized AI agents inside customer accounts. Anthropic is not immune here, as its own S-1 makes it clear the company is keen to add more customer agents.
Whether the risk factors outlined in Anthropic’s S-1 are unusually candid or boilerplate, they expose a gap in regulation. The states, for their part, are trying to fill it. California’s SB53, for instance , which took effect in January, requires large AI developers to report critical safety incidents within fifteen days, while New York’s RAISE Act (which takes full effect at the start of 2027) requires the same reporting within 72 hours. But both laws were written with catastrophe in mind, not a slow-moving public health crisis fostered by chatbots that deepens a teenager’s delusions or hands out users’ personal information over the web without consent .
