Evacuation comes weeks after US withdrew bombers from RAF Fairford over suspected Iran-linked security incident
The US military has reportedly evacuated aircraft from a second airbase in ⁠Britain after a threat from Iran.
Two US refuelling tankers that were using the RAF Mildenhall military base diverted to Germany on Monday morning, while several other tankers at the base ⁠were moved to Germany and other locations later in the day, according to the Wall Street Journal.
Washington withdrew its bombers from ⁠RAF Fairford airbase in September over ⁠a suspected Iran-linked ​security incident .
The precise nature of the threat to RAF Mildenhall remained ⁠under discussion among US officials, it was reported.
The cabinet minister Lucy Powell said the security of military bases in the UK was constantly under review. She told Sky News she could not comment on live operations, “but we’re constantly keeping the security of our bases under review and, as we’ve seen with other cases recently, we take firm and quick action where we need to”.
A Ministry of Defence spokesperson said: “We do not routinely comment on the activity of other nations. Aircraft and other assets move regularly according to operational requirements.”
The US had upgraded the security threat level at RAF Mildenhall and RAF Lakenheath, the report said, citing a US ‌official familiar with the ‌matter.
The base was placed under Force Protection Condition (FPCON) Charlie, which is the second-highest defensive threat level in the US Department of Defense’s security system ‌and occurs when intelligence indicates a form of terrorist action is likely.
It is understood that, on the ground, there has been no specific threat against the RAF base. No arrests have been made, suggesting the threat seen by the US was more general.
A US Air Force spokesperson said: “US Air Force aircraft rotate between installations and operating locations for a variety of reasons, including training and real world requirements. US military aircraft are hosted in accordance with access, basing, and overflight agreements with our allies and partners. Due to operations security, we will not provide further information on movement of assets.”

Five men were arrested outside RAF Fairford airbase in Gloucestershire in September over a suspected plot to attack the base.
Two men, Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, and Nouman Essghir, 24, who were not among the men arrested at RAF Fairford, later appeared in court charged under the National Security Act 2023 in connection with the incident. Abdulkarim, from Westminster, was charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service, which police earlier said they believed to be Iran.
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said ‌last month that ​the activity at RAF Fairford ​was likely to have been coordinated in Iran .
While Tehran’s ambassador to Britain has denied accusations it was involved in any plot against the airbase, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said in July that Fairford and any other bases used to launch attacks against Iran were legitimate targets.

articles.title_orig: Thick smog shrouds New Delhi after Diwali firecrackers add to seasonal pollution
articles.title_zh: Thick smog shrouds New Delhi after Diwali firecrackers add to seasonal pollution
articles.content_orig:
There are two cardboard boxes in Meenu Rana's living room in Delhi. One is filled with Diwali decorations and twinkling lights. The other holds air purifiers.
"The mornings have already started feeling stuffy. It will get worse in the coming days, so it's better to be prepared," says the 43-year-old teacher.
She is not alone. Every year, as winter and the festive season approach, residents of India's capital begin preparing for something far less celebratory: months of breathing polluted air.
Delhi and its satellite cities record some of the world's highest pollution levels through the year. But as winter sets in, the air often becomes unbearable.
Falling temperatures and slower winds trap pollutants close to the ground instead of allowing them to disperse. Smoke from crop residue burning in neighbouring states adds to emissions from vehicles and factories, as well as construction dust. Firecrackers used during festivals often worsen air quality.
The result is noxious air and a familiar question: why does pollution return year after year, and why hasn't more been done to tackle it?
This year, however, the Delhi government announced its Winter Action Plan months before the worst of the smog arrived. The plan is in place from 1 November to 28 February, covering the months when pollution usually spikes.
Experts have called this a step in the right direction, noting that in previous years measures were often rolled out only after the air quality got too bad to ignore. However, they say this by itself won't be enough, calling for more holistic, long-lasting measures.
Just days after the plan came into effect, the city is slipping back into a depressingly familiar pattern .
This week, a grey haze hangs over Delhi, along with a distinct smoky smell that residents unwillingly recognise. People complain of irritation in their eyes and difficulty breathing, and coughs and sneezes are heard everywhere.
For those who can afford them, air purifiers have become a household necessity. Outdoors, people wear masks or cover their faces with cloth, trying to protect themselves from the worst of the pollution.
Tackling pollution was among the promises made by the governing Bharatiya Janata Party during its election campaign last year. Its winter action plan is now a major test of that pledge.
The plan restricts the entry of older, more polluting vehicles registered outside Delhi and denies fuel to vehicles without a certificate which shows they meet emission standards. Demolitions and outdoor construction work that generate dust have been temporarily banned.
Private vehicle use is being discouraged - the government has asked offices to allow half of their employees to work from home, introduced staggered office timings for its staff and doubled parking charges. It says it will also strengthen pollution monitoring and enforcement and promote public transport and electric vehicles.
These measures are separate from the Graded Response Action Plan (Grap), which is overseen by the federal Commission for Air Quality Management.
Grap introduces restrictions in stages, with stricter measures kicking in as pollution levels rise. This week, its second stage is in force, restricting the use of diesel generators and burning of coal and firewood.
Experts say on paper, these actions collectively provide a roadmap for responding to rising pollution levels but their success ultimately depends on enforcement.
"There are a lot of positive changes as far as planning is concerned, but when it comes to execution, we probably still stand at the same level," says Parthaa Bosu, strategic adviser at the Environmental Defense Fund, a non-profit group focused on delivering climate solutions.
Others argue that the problem goes much deeper.
"If we want to reduce pollution, we need to set targets for every sector - including power generation, industry and transport - not just vehicle entry, construction and stubble burning," says Manoj Kumar, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.
"We know how much each sector and each state contributes to pollution. We can set targets to reduce emissions from each of them over the next five years."
Bosu points out that an issue which does not get enough attention is secondary pollutants - when gases in the air react with sunlight, water vapour and other substances to form harmful particles that contribute to pollution.
"Pollution is not just caused by biomass burning or vehicles," he says. "Dust being stirred up from the ground, coal and fly ash, materials burned at brick kilns and the large-scale burning of urban waste are also contributing to the problem. And much of this is still not being stopped."
Delhi's pollution problem is also affected by what happens outside the city . Pollutants travel into Delhi from neighbouring states and other parts of northern India, worsening the situation, Bosu explains.
This means that measures taken by Delhi can achieve only so much. Tackling the problem requires neighbouring states and the wider northern region to work together, he adds.
In the meantime, pollution is harming people's health every day.
During winter, government monitoring stations in Delhi frequently record Air Quality Index (AQI) readings above 300, classified as "very poor".
On particularly bad days, readings can reach 500, the highest point on India's scale. That does not mean pollution cannot rise further, only that domestic trackers do not record it. International trackers such as Swiss-based IQAir have recorded readings close to 1,000 on some days.
The World Health Organization recommends average PM2.5 levels over 24 hours should not exceed 15 micrograms per cubic metre. In Delhi, levels are often at more than 25 times that limit during pollution season.
Dr Manoj Goel, pulmonology unit head at Fortis Memorial Research Institute near Delhi, says these tiny particles "can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream, triggering inflammation and affecting multiple organs".
Even short-term exposure can cause throat irritation, coughing, wheezing and breathlessness. It can also worsen existing heart and lung conditions.
A 2025 report by the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago estimated that air pollution could reduce life expectancy in Delhi by up to 8.2 years.
For residents, the challenge is not just limited to breathing. The restrictions also disrupt everyday life.
Delhi is closely connected to its satellite towns, Noida and Gurugram, with thousands of people travelling between them every day for work. Long queues form at the city's borders as vehicles are stopped and checked, leaving commuters stuck in traffic for hours.
While the new rules offer some hope, frustration is growing.
Protests, political arguments and court interventions have become part of the annual cycle. But despite public pressure and government measures, the pollution returns every winter.
Rana keeps her windows closed and curtains drawn, and has added more indoor plants.
The arrival of another winter fills her family with dread, but unlike many others , they are not planning to move out of Delhi.
"I would have left the city long ago had there been an option, but my son has his school, my husband and I have our jobs as well, which makes it practically impossible," she says.
"What option do we have? It is unfair but we will have to live with it."

articles.title_orig: US demands a seat for Europe at Ukraine peace talks
articles.title_zh: US demands a seat for Europe at Ukraine peace talks
articles.content_orig:
ABU DHABI — European governments’ long-running and sometimes bad-tempered debate over who should represent them in Ukraine peace talks just became urgent.
Donald Trump’s envoys are pressing Russia to allow Europe to join the next round of negotiations aimed at resolving the Ukraine war, according to U.S. officials granted anonymity to discuss sensitive matters.
Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff will push the case for Europe to have a direct role in future talks as they mediate the first trilateral discussion with Russia and Ukraine since February in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday, the officials said.
European governments and EU institutions will likely not have long to decide who they want at the negotiating table on their behalf. Kushner and Witkoff want to step up the pace of the talks and for this week’s meeting to be the last without Europe’s full participation, the same officials said.
“We need Europe at the table,” one of the officials said. “So our proposal is to bring the Europeans into the discussion after this trilateral.”
The officials welcomed the fact that the leaders of Finland and Norway called Russia’s Vladimir Putin directly on Oct. 27 and said more outreach is necessary. “We need a lot more European discussions with Russia so that they could be hearing what we’re hearing and the message that they’re conveying to us they could be conveying to Russia directly.”
The question of who speaks for Europe — and whether Ukraine’s European allies should even be speaking to Putin at all — has been deeply divisive . EU leaders will discuss the topic at an informal summit in Dublin later this week.
Ever since Trump returned to the White House last year, EU officials and diplomats have been fretting about being left on the sidelines while the U.S. talks directly to Russia to negotiate an end to the war.
Senior European officials are due in Abu Dhabi for the meetings this week but, although Kushner and Witkoff are expected to consult them, they will not be involved in the main negotiations due to Russian objections. Those present include security advisers from the U.K., Germany, France, as well as officials from Italy, NATO, the European Commission and European Council.
The U.S. officials said Day 1 of the talks would focus on security guarantees for Ukraine and the potential reshaping of the security architecture of Europe. Day 2 would look at territorial issues — where the borders and boundaries should be drawn — and other questions.
European governments fear that Trump may be preparing to agree to longstanding demands from Putin to roll back NATO’s influence in the region. But the U.S. officials insisted that NATO would still be central to Europe’s collective defense, while refusing to back away from the need for a fundamental rethink of the continent’s relations with Russia.
“Obviously something’s not working,” the same official said. Europeans have “a lot of baggage” about redrawing the security architecture because Russia had proposed various changes in the past and previous arrangements had failed, the official said. “We have to build something new that works today.”
The officials said NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte had been heavily involved in the discussions with the U.S. administration and in sharing ideas for reforms.
On the most difficult question of all for Ukraine — the fate of Russian-occupied territory — both sides have shown “flexibility” in private, the officials said. The aim of this week’s talks is to keep up the momentum of recent weeks, rather than to deliver a final ceasefire, they added.
But the two main tracks in the talks — territory and future security arrangements for Ukraine and Europe — must run together and be resolved together, the U.S. side said.
Additional reporting by Scott Waldman.

Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment
A prominent Russian milblogger noted that the Russian Ministry of Defense (MoD) has recently issued fewer claims of Russian forces seizing settlements in Ukraine. The milblogger acknowledged on November 8 that the rate of Russian MoD claims of seizing settlements had recently decreased significantly, marking a notable shift in the pattern of Russian MoD reporting.[1] The Russian MoD and Chief of the General Staff Army General Valery Gerasimov collectively claimed that Russian forces seized 38 settlements across the frontline in October 2026 alone.[2] The Russian MoD claimed the seizure of Vasylkove (northwest of Hulyaipole and 18 kilometers from the nearest Russian advance or infiltration area) on November 9, marking the first Russian MoD claim of seizing a settlement since October 28.[3] The prominent Russian milblogger assessed that this shift may suggest that Russian forces have difficulty fighting in colder weather or that Russian MoD officials conducted a “non-public revision” of the current frontline after receiving exaggerated battlefield reports from military commanders. The milblogger assessed that the Russian MoD may also have felt compelled to respond to accurate reporting that the rate of Russian advances has decreased significantly in 2026 compared to 2025.[4] Russian forces lost ground on the battlefield in both September and October 2026, highlighting the increasingly stark contrast between the Kremlin‘s cognitive warfare campaign to portray Ukrainian defenses as on the verge of collapsing and the actual battlefield reality.[5] This shift in Russian MoD reporting may also indicate that the MoD is leaning into the Kremlin’s new theory of victory in Ukraine, which now relies on a deadly and destructive long-range drone and missile campaign against Ukrainian energy and critical infrastructure over the upcoming Winter 2026-2027 to compel Ukraine into surrender.[6]
The Russian Central Bank is acknowledging that Russia’s war in Ukraine is having mounting economic effect, while trying to present these effects as temporary. Russian Central Bank Chairperson Elvira Nabiullina stated on November 9 to the Russian State Duma that there should be no rush to lower the key interest rate (which the Central Bank has lowered 10 times since June 2025) as Russia continues to experience significant inflation.[7] Nabiullina acknowledged that Ukrainian strikes against oil refineries, data centers, logistics hubs, and other industrial facilities have constrained Russian production capacity, but claimed that Russian officials are addressing these “temporary” challenges. Nabiullina stated that the gap between the inflation rate and the key interest rate reflects persistent inflationary pressure and the large share of subsidized loans in Russia. Nabiullina added that the Russian Central Bank will continue to lower the key interest rate in 2027 but that it will remain in the double digits. Ukraine’s long-range strike campaigns against Russian energy infrastructure and the recent strikes against Russian logistics facilities — the effects of which Nabiullina acknowledged — are generating additional inflationary pressures on the already-strained Russian economy.[8] Russian authorities thus far have failed to adequately protect their critical infrastructure or quickly repair damage from Ukrainian strikes and are unlikely to be able to rapidly address these issues ahead of or into 2027, the timeline that Nabiullina insinuated.[9]
Nabiullina’s characterization of Russia’s economic strains as temporary contrasts with the Kremlin’s preparations for increased budget deficits over the coming years and the mounting costs of wartime economic policies for ordinary Russians. The Ukrainian Foreign Intelligence Service (SZRU) reported on November 6 that the Russian State Duma Committee on Budget and Taxes recognized the risk of a shortfall in federal budget revenues for 2027-2029, forecasting an annual deficit of between $63.6 to $67.6 billion or around 1.9-2.2 percent of Russia’s GDP.[10] The SZRU reported that the Russian federal government also plans to increase public debt from $56.7 billion in 2027 to $70.5 billion in 2029. The SZRU noted that the Russian government nonetheless plans to spend more than $212 billion on defense in 2027. The SZRU reported on November 8 that 28 percent of all borrowers in Russian banks were struggling to service loans as of August 2026, while 33 companies entered into technical default (a breach of a loan’s terms and conditions that does not involve missed payments), of which 17 eventually entered full default, between January and September 2026.[11] The SZRU noted that wage debt reached over 2.5 billion rubles (roughly $30.3 million) by the end of September 2026, while regular Russians have been increasingly relying on debt to pay for basic necessities, including heating. A Russian milblogger claimed on November 9 that hardships and inconveniences are inevitable for Russians in the fifth year of war and encouraged Russians to focus on buying generators and stockpiling fuel, water, food, and medicine.[12]
These economically sub-optimal policies to continue funding the Kremlin’s war in Ukraine will have long-term economic implications.[13]  Russia is experiencing labor shortages that have caused wage inflation in the civilian and defense sectors, contributing to overall inflation.[14] Russia has also been increasingly struggling with liquidity problems and high levels of external debt after having steadily depleted its sovereign wealth fund’s liquid reserves to fund its war in Ukraine.[15] Russian civilians have also experienced severe fuel shortages and price spikes throughout Summer 2026, further straining already tight budgets while fueling inflation.[16] Russian President Vladimir Putin has nonetheless continuously pressured the Russian Central Bank to lower the key interest rate as part of Putin’s efforts to impose a looser monetary policy in order to expand capital and liquidity availability for the Russian military and defense industry.[17]
Russian forces continue to lean into highly maneuverable quasi-cruise missiles for strike packages against Ukraine’s critical and industrial infrastructure, exploiting Ukrainian air defense and interceptor shortages. Ukraine’s Main Military Intelligence Directorate (GUR) reported on November 9 that Russia is fielding a new modification of the Geran-5 long-range strike drone — the Geran-5 K5-K — which the GUR classified as a “small sized cruise missile” due to its aerodynamics and technical characteristics.[18] The GUR reported that the Geran-5 K5-K is shorter and has a narrower wingspan than a typical Geran-5, has a maximum cruising speed of 450 kilometers per hour, has a 1,000-kilometer range, and carries a 90-kilogram warhead.[19] The GUR stated that Russia has already fielded Geran-5 K5-K drones with a thermobaric warhead — an adaptation likely intended to maximize damage, which disproportionately affects civilian areas in Ukraine.[20] Russian forces began integrating inexpensive, highly maneuverable quasi-cruise missiles, including Banderols and Dan-Ts, into their strike packages in mid-2026, likely to exploit Ukraine’s air defense interceptor shortages before Ukraine can effectively field a counter to such weapons.[21] Quasi-cruise missiles bridge the gap between slow and inexpensive strike drones and cruise missiles, and modifying a Geran-type drone in this way will likely further confuse and pressure strained Ukrainian air defenses. Russia will likely continue to prioritize the development of quasi-cruise missiles, jet-powered drones, and other more destructive variants of its strike drones in order to devastate Ukraine’s logistics, transportation, and energy infrastructure going into the Winter 2026-2027 strike campaign.[22]

articles.title_orig: Why COP31 may be the EU’s last great climate hurrah
articles.title_zh: Why COP31 may be the EU’s last great climate hurrah
articles.content_orig:
ANTALYA, Turkey—The stench of fossil fuels has become a hallmark of the United Nations “Conference of the Parties” climate talks, starting with the airplanes and buses carrying delegates to the conferences.
Two annual meetings have been held in Poland, where coal remains king. Eye-searing petrochemical smog marred the skies over Dubai at COP28. In Baku, Azerbaijan, most buildings are coated with gray grime from refinery pollution, and last year at the “Nature COP” in Belém, Brazil, hundreds of diesel generators ran day and night outside the conference halls in a futile effort to cool the heavy tropical air.
The latest iteration of the negotiations, COP31, opened Monday here with diesel fumes in the city’s busy streets providing another reminder that the world remains deeply dependent on the fossil fuels driving the climate crisis even after three decades of climate negotiations.
The backdrop to this year’s conference is bleak. Scientists report that the average global temperature has reached a record high of more than 3.6 degrees Fahrenheit (2 degrees Celsius) above the preindustrial baseline in the last few days. Several dozen glaciers have disappeared since last year’s talks. Rising seas are flooding coastal cities. And carbon dioxide emissions in 2026 are on track to reach another record high.
The climate crisis didn’t reach this point overnight, said Marc Hudson , an unaffiliated climate researcher in the United Kingdom. It is the culmination of decades of missed opportunities, political compromises and broken promises. Understanding how it happened requires revisiting a surreal and occasionally absurd history, he said.
A convenient starting point is 1957, when scientists from around the world shared research and met repeatedly to study Earth as a system, rather than individual components, as part of the International Geophysical Year . It was also when American scientist Charles Keeling began developing a system to measure the rise of CO2 in the global atmosphere, and when a landmark research paper challenged the assumption that the oceans could absorb CO2 emissions from fossil fuel burning.
It’s clear from the scientific record, Hudson said, that researchers understood the looming problem nearly 70 years ago.
But the issue did not appear on political radar screens until 1985, when scientists at an international climate conference in Austria warned that rising CO2 levels could produce climate warming greater than any in human history, with significant consequences for agriculture, ecosystems and people.
The researchers urged governments to start considering policy responses. A few years later, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change was born. In 1990, the panel issued its first major climate assessment , spurring the United Nations to action.
Representatives from more than 140 countries spent 15 months negotiating the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change . At that point, about 10 industrialized countries were responsible for about 80 percent of all historic CO2 emissions. There was broad agreement that those nations should take the lead in reducing climate-altering pollution and that any treaty should not deny poorer countries the chance to develop.
That disagreement remains one of the defining features of climate diplomacy, and the United States has been central to that debate since the beginning, Hudson said. George H.W. Bush, a former fossil-fuel industry executive, was president, and he was “even more sympathetic than the Democrats to big auto, big oil,” Hudson said. The Bush administration feared that the international community would mobilize against carbon dioxide emissions in much the same way it had against ozone depletion just a few years earlier.
France and a few other European countries pushed for a treaty that would obligate rich, industrialized countries to set timetables for emission cuts, but it was “very important for the Americans and the Saudis and the Gulf oil and gas exporters that whatever deal emerged from an international negotiating process was as weak as possible,” Hudson said. Bush threatened to boycott the 1992 Rio Earth Summit if a treaty included binding language on emissions cuts.
The French and other proponents of emissions-reduction targets had to choose between pressing ahead with a strong treaty that the U.S. wouldn’t sign or watering down the agreement to secure American support.
“This was straightforward, naked power politics,” Hudson said. “The Americans and the Saudis wanted to make sure that they could keep on selling and using fossil fuels for as long as they wanted, and they didn’t want to have to negotiate on actual emissions reductions.”
In the final weeks of negotiations for the U.N. Framework Convention on Climate Change agreement, references to binding cuts were removed from the draft and the U.S. became an early signatory because it was “no longer worried about what was becoming a toothless agreement,” and setting the stage for the first Conference of the Parties, COP1, in Berlin, Hudson said.
The climate framework was vague, but it included an agreement to try to stabilize emissions at 1990 levels. Most people involved in the talks hoped a more detailed agreement with timetables and national plans would soon follow, said Joanna Depledge , a climate diplomacy researcher at the University of Cambridge.
Most probably never would have believed that emissions would still be increasing 30 years later, she added.
The early international steps toward tackling global warming came after the end of the Cold War, as former adversaries sought to cooperate, she said.

But then, as now, she added, the U.S. was reluctant to accept an agreement that would put the onus on developed countries to reduce emissions first and was reluctant to assume any financial obligations toward developing countries. This worldview has continued shaping the climate talks for 30 years.
At COP1 in Berlin in 1995, delegates acknowledged that the U.N.’s climate framework alone would not solve the emerging global warming problem, so they agreed to keep meeting to reach a follow-up deal with quantifiable emission-reduction targets for industrialized countries. Since then, the 198 countries party to the climate framework have met 29 more times to try and implement those basic ideas.
Just two years later, the Kyoto Protocol, with obligatory emissions reductions for industrialized countries, was adopted at COP3. But just before the conference, the U.S. Senate passed the Byrd-Hagel Resolution by a vote of 95–0, declaring that it would not ratify an agreement on emissions cuts that did not require similar commitments from developing countries, or that would harm the U.S. economy.
President Bill Clinton signed the agreement in 1998, which may have been a high-water mark for U.S. engagement in the process, at least until the Paris Agreement was adopted in 2015, Depledge said. But Clinton never sent it to the Senate.
In 2001, his successor, President George W. Bush, said the U.S. would not ratify the Kyoto Protocol, taking momentum away from the global push to curb global warming.

articles.title_orig: The Dow Just Jumped 1,100 Points. Here's What Warren Buffett's 2008 Rule Says to a 66-Year-Old Retiree Who Almost Moved $600,000 to Cash on Friday - 24/7 Wall St.
articles.title_zh: The Dow Just Jumped 1,100 Points. Here's What Warren Buffett's 2008 Rule Says to a 66-Year-Old Retiree Who Almost Moved $600,000 to Cash on Friday - 24/7 Wall St.
articles.content_orig:
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped about 1,100 points on Monday, and Warren Buffett’s rule for exactly this moment is 18 years old: “So if you wait for the robins, spring will be over.” He wrote it in The New York Times on Oct. 17, 2008, a month after Lehman Brothers failed, in a piece titled “Buy American. I Am.” The sentence before it said what he meant: “What is likely, however, is that the market will move higher, perhaps substantially so, well before either sentiment or the economy turns up.”
Monday fit the rule. The Dow rose more than 2% to roughly 52,400. The S&P 500 index fund rose 2.4%, its biggest gain since April 8, and the Nasdaq-100 fund rose 3.5%. That came three trading days after the S&P 500 fund’s 4.4% drop on Thursday, its worst day since April 2025, and one trading day after stocks closed their worst week since the tariff week of April 2025. The worries that drove last week’s selling had not been settled over the weekend. The main change on Monday was a drop in oil prices.
Monday’s 1,100 points are a warning about the cost of waiting for the all-clear: the rebound came while the worries that caused the selling were still there, which is what Buffett’s rule says to expect. They are also one day, and one day says nothing about whether last Thursday was the low.
Take a retired couple, 66 and 63, with $1.8 million: $1,250,000 in a rollover IRA, $400,000 in a brokerage account and $150,000 in a Roth. They hold 65% in an S&P 500 index fund, $1,170,000 at Friday’s close, and $630,000 in bonds and a money market fund. Social Security pays them $4,800 a month, $57,600 a year, and they spend $118,000, so they draw $60,400 a year from the portfolio, 3.4% of it. On Friday afternoon, after a week of headlines, he typed an order to move $600,000 of the IRA’s index fund to cash, the money market fund, until things settled down. He did not send it. If you typed something like it, here is what the order would have cost by Monday’s close, what Buffett’s rule cost the people who followed it in 2008 before it paid them, and the one number that should decide this for you instead of the Dow.
Their stock sleeve was worth $1,239,695 at the S&P 500’s Oct. 6 record. Thursday took $53,799 out of it in one session. It closed Friday at $1,170,000 and Monday at $1,197,607, a gain of $27,607 in a day, and it is still $42,087 under the record.
The $600,000 that was almost in the money market fund would have missed $14,158 of Monday’s gain. That is one day. The larger cost is the one Buffett’s sentence describes. If you sell until it settles down, you need a signal that it has settled, and the usual one is the index back at its record. The S&P 500 fund’s record is 6.0% above Friday’s close, so $600,000 that waits for that signal buys back $566,268 worth of Friday’s shares, $33,732 less, and only if the record is the first sign of calm. In exchange, the money market fund would pay you about 4.17%, the 3-month Treasury bill rate: $25,020 a year, or $2,085 a month.
Buffett was careful to say what the rule does not do. “Let me be clear on one point: I can’t predict the short-term movements of the stock market,” he wrote, and he was right to be careful. He published on Oct. 17, 2008, with the S&P 500 fund at $93.21. It kept falling for five months, to $68.11 on March 9, 2009, a loss of 26.9% after his piece ran. If you had bought that week because of it, you were down by more than a quarter by spring.
Then the robins came late, exactly as he said. The recession ended in June 2009, but the National Bureau of Economic Research did not announce that until Sept. 20, 2010, and by that day the fund had risen 67.7% from its low. A year after the piece ran, the fund was up 17.8% from where he published. Five years after, 85.8%. Today it is 8.07 times the price on the day it ran, price only, with dividends excluded: $100,000 held through all of it is $807,467. The same $100,000 rolled in 3-month Treasury bills since that day is $129,634. His other line in the piece was about that choice: “Today people who hold cash equivalents feel comfortable. They shouldn’t.”
The reason the rule works is in the calendar of the S&P 500 fund’s daily closes since 2000. Of its 20 best days in that span, 12 came within 10 trading days of one of its 20 worst days. The two biggest, Oct. 13, 2008 (up 14.5%) and Oct. 28, 2008 (up 11.7%), landed in the middle of the worst stretch of the crisis. The third biggest, April 9, 2025 (up 10.5%), came three trading days after the tariff drop that still marks the last week worse than the one just ended.
That clustering is what a sell-and-wait order buys you. $100,000 put in the fund on Jan. 3, 2000, and left alone was worth $517,501 on Monday, 6.31% a year, price only. If you missed the 10 best days, you have $224,552, 3.06% a year. If you missed the 20 best, you have $131,516, 1.03% a year, less than the $169,619 that 3-month Treasury bills returned over the same stretch. Those 20 days are fewer than one a year, and most of them fell in the weeks when you would most have wanted to be out.
The rule says the recovery arrives before the all-clear. It does not say when, and it does not say Monday was the start of it. In 2008 the fund fell another 26.9% after Buffett wrote, and the 1,100 points the Dow gained on Monday leave the S&P 500 fund 3.4% below its record and the Nasdaq-100 fund 10.6% below its own. If you draw $60,400 a year, you cannot wait five years for the robins with money you need next year, and Buffett was writing about his personal account, which he said had held nothing but Treasury bonds until then.
That is why the decision for this couple belongs to a different number than the Dow. Their $630,000 outside stocks covers 10.4 years of draws at $60,400 a year. The 2007 to 2009 fall took the S&P 500 fund 5.4 years to repair, from its October 2007 peak to the first close above it in March 2013, and the 2000 to 2002 fall took 7.2 years. A reserve that covers a decade means no stock has to be sold in a bad year, which is the only thing the Friday order was trying to buy, at a cost of $14,158 on its first day. If your real worry is the mix, that 65% in stocks is more than you can sleep with at 66, change it once, inside the IRA where it costs you nothing in tax, and pick the day from your plan, which does not care what the Dow did on Monday.
The Dow rose about 1,100 points on Monday, the S&P 500 fund had its biggest day since April 8, and the worries that caused last week’s selling were still there when it happened. That is the moment Buffett’s 2008 rule describes: the market moves first, the news catches up later, and the people who wait for the robins miss spring. His rule cost its followers 26.9% in the five months after he wrote it and paid them 85.8% within five years. For a couple with $1.8 million, the $600,000 order that was never sent would have missed $14,158 on Monday and $33,732 of shares if they waited for the record to buy back. The number that should settle it for you is 10.4 years, the draws their bonds and cash already cover, and that number was the same on Thursday night as it is tonight.

articles.title_orig: US-Iran war: Trump says more US attacks on Iran 'highly unlikely'
articles.title_zh: US-Iran war: Trump says more US attacks on Iran 'highly unlikely'
articles.content_orig:
Donald Trump has said "Iran militarily is effectively over", and said that there is "positive momentum" behind negotiations to end the Middle East conflict.
"We're just keeping it the status quo," the US president said on Monday. "And we're doing that really at the behest of countries that are their neighbours."
Addressing reporters from the White House press briefing room, Trump said that renewed US attacks on Iran were "highly unlikely" but that the US was "locked and loaded" should the circumstances change.
Iranian officials have repeatedly expressed doubts about Trump's prior comments about resolving the conflict.
This is not the first time that Trump has said the Iran war is "militarily" over, but the circumstances for him are different now.
The president has hinted at de-escalation in Iran after a bruising set of midterm election results for the Republicans last week, which senior figures including Vice-President JD Vance blamed on the Iran war.
Ahead of the midterms, Trump had said US forces conducted what he described as "minor strikes" on an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz . However, in an interview with 60 Minutes that aired on Sunday, the president said that he did not currently see "any reason" to escalate the conflict.
Responding to a question over why he would not officially declare an end to the war, Trump said that some of the Gulf allies could still face Iranian aggression.
"We have some great allies there and we have to make sure they're not hurt," he said, suggesting that the US naval blockade on Iranian ports was helping to make the region more secure.
Global oil prices, which have fallen sharply since the midterms, dipped further after Trump's comments.
On Tuesday afternoon in Asia, Brent crude was more than 1% lower at $91.50 (£52) while US-traded was down by 1.2% at $85.82.
Trump hosted Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdul Rahman Al Thani in the Oval Office earlier on Monday, saying they had an "excellent conversation" about negotiations to end the war.
In a post on X, the Qatari leader said he held "positive discussions" with Trump and Vance on "reaching a deal and bringing peace to the region".
Efforts to broker a peace between Washington and Tehran have largely been held indirectly through mediators since the war first broke out following joint US-Israeli strikes in February.
Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates are among the US's Gulf allies that have been hit by Iranian strikes over the course of the war, in addition to the threat of strikes that have led to major air travel disruptions in the region.
Post-election recriminations over the US war in Iran are already placing pressure on members of the Trump administration.
Republican congressman Thomas Massie launched a strong attack against Trump's Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday over the war in Iran, requesting a vote in the House of Representatives to impeach him.
Trump has backed Hegseth, who says he is "not worried" about the looming impeachment threats, calling Massie's effort a "sham".
While the move is unlikely to succeed with Republicans still in control of Congress until January, Democrats have expressed willingness to impeach Hegseth once the new session begins and they have control of both the House and the Senate.

articles.title_orig: 'Cruise for life' ship seized in Singapore
articles.title_zh: 'Cruise for life' ship seized in Singapore
articles.content_orig:
A round-the-world cruise that left passengers stranded in Cambodia after its US-based operator ran out of money has been seized in Singapore.
The Odyssey, which set off from Belfast in October 2024 and was meant to take guests on a years-long voyage around the world, is now anchored in Singapore port waters, local authorities say.
Around 200 guests were forced to leave the ship last month in the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville, after its owner Villa Vie Residences abruptly suspended operations citing "extraordinary increases in fuel costs".
The crew onboard are reported to be well, Singapore's port authority said.
"Arrangements for their welfare and wellbeing are being managed by the vessel's creditors," the authority said, adding that the vessel had been "placed under arrest pursuant to a court order".
Singapore law firm Helmsman LLC has been named the "arresting solicitor", but it is not clear which party it represents.
The Odyssey was meant to go on a three-and-a-half-years voyage covering 150 countries.
Passengers were given the options of buying their cabin outright, which allows them to stay onboard beyond its initial voyage, paying for a five-year residency, or renting a cabin for days-long tours.
Permanent residencies in its cabins ranged from $120,000 (£89,272) to $440,000. Those cabins were also available for rent from $3,500 a month, according to its website.
"For roughly the price of a car, you can own your home on a ship that travels the world," its founder Mikael Petterson had earlier said.
However the cruise was beset with problems from the start, with its departure delayed for four months because of repairs and paperwork.
While in Vietnam, crew members reportedly bought food from local grocery stores because the company owed money to a vendor who refused to deliver food, according to CBS News, the BBC's partner in the US.
CBS also reported that the operator warned passengers of its financial troubles in August, when it had sailed on a separate occasion into Singapore, and had to raise money from guests to keep the cruise going.
It had also mentioned the risk of being detained then.
Holly Hennessey, one of the ship's passengers, had earlier told the BBC guests were asked to consider paying a fuel surcharge as prices soared, and that their itinerary had been "severely curtailed".
The vessel sailed again into Singapore earlier this month, weeks after the cruise came to a sudden end while in Cambodia.
As the Iran war sent fuel prices soaring earlier this year, monthly fuel cost per cabin in parts of Asia had risen to as much as $8,000 from $1,800, Villa Vie Residences said in a statement on 27 October.
It added that it had taken "significant steps to reduce fuel consumption" but those measures turned out to be insufficient to offset the "extraordinary increase in fuel costs".
The company also said it was working with residents to "identify temporary living arrangements" while in Cambodia.

articles.title_orig: After meeting Qatar PM, Trump calls Iran war ‘effectively over’ militarily
articles.title_zh: After meeting Qatar PM, Trump calls Iran war ‘effectively over’ militarily
articles.content_orig:
United States President Donald Trump has signalled that he considers the US-Israel war on Iran “effectively” at an end, after meeting Qatar’s prime minister in Washington, DC.
In a surprise briefing on Monday, Trump reiterated his position that the US had destroyed Iran’s military. But his remarks suggested he faces pressure from allies in the Middle East to bring hostilities to a close.
“Iran militarily is effectively over,” he said. “We’re just keeping it the status quo, and we’re doing that really at the behest of countries that are their neighbours.”
His comments followed a closed-door meeting with US Vice President JD Vance and Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani, who hailed the progress in a post on social media.
“We discussed the situation in the region and ways to progress the US-Iran talks,” the prime minister said. “Grateful for the positive discussions on reaching a deal and bringing peace to the region.”
Still, Trump acknowledged the “status quo” would involve continuing the US naval blockade against Iranian ports, as well as the newly announced Task Force Iron Gate, which seeks to cut off trade by land and through the Caspian Sea.
“Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait and others would prefer the status quo, that we remain as is,” he said. “In other words, a continuation of the greatest naval blockade in the history of our country. Probably in the history of the world.”
Trump also indicated in his briefing that the US was willing to resume fighting, should the need arise.
“Taking military action doesn’t seem to be a very necessary thing, but we’re locked and loaded, ready to go for any reason that changes,” he said.
“Israel and the entire Middle East are protected from Iranian danger and threats, and we’re seeing momentum toward the end of this conflict. I think it’s going to be ending fairly soon.”
Iranian officials, meanwhile, dismissed Trump’s latest remarks as a distraction.
“The war on Iran has already wrecked the US government. But Washington flails like a desperate gambler,” Iran’s Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei wrote in a post on social media.
“FOLD YOUR HAND. STOP manufacturing FAKE NEWS about imaginary talks.”
Separately, Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian said that the country’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei had called for an end to the situation, which he described as “neither war nor peace”.
Pezeshkian added that Iran was open to further negotiations but would not be coerced, according to Iranian media. “We will not surrender to force and bullying,” he said.
Since the war on Iran began on February 28, the conflict has spilled into surrounding countries and roiled international trade.
Almost as soon as the US and Israel began their attacks, Iran moved to shut down the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for oil, gas and fertiliser, among other goods.
Iran also responded to US and Israeli strikes with missile and drone fire on its neighbours in the Gulf, including Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait and the UAE, with many of the attacks targeting US military installations.
Other, related conflicts have since emerged. Saudi Arabia has renewed its fight against the Iran-backed Houthis, and Israel began its occupation of southern Lebanon, as well as deadly air strikes.
In the nearly nine months since the war began, the US offensive against Iran has grown sporadic, with intermittent exchanges of fire.
In recent days, for instance, the Trump administration announced “minor strikes” against Iran’s Qeshm Island.
It also offered a $20m reward for “information about Iran’s nuclear program, including its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel”.
After the Twelve-Day War in June 2025, Trump had claimed that Iran’s uranium enrichment programme had been obliterated. But he has since made curtailing Iran’s nuclear programme a central premise for the ongoing war.
Iran has long denied seeking a nuclear weapon, maintaining its uranium enrichment programme is for the purposes of civilian energy generation.
Officials in Iran, meanwhile, have pushed for the US to accept seven conditions in order to end the war.
They include lifting US sanctions, releasing frozen Iranian funds, recognising a new shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz worked out with Oman, and ending the war on all fronts, including Israel’s attacks on Lebanon.
Qatar has served as one of several key mediators in the conflict. Sheikh Mohammed, the prime minister, also serves as foreign minister and has been known to act as an intermediary between Washington and Tehran.
In Monday’s closed-door meeting, he reportedly presented Trump with a two-day proposal from Iran to end the war.
Afterwards, reporters asked Trump in the briefing room, “Why not just declare an end to the conflict and be done with it?”
Trump replied by framing the continued US blockade as a question of regional security. He also called for a “long-term solution”, rather than a short-term one.
“We have some great allies there, and we have to make sure they’re not hurt, and they would be hurt,” he said.
“They are right now a lot safer than they were six months ago because Iran’s been very much decapitated. But they’re still the bully of the Middle East a little bit.”

Anthropic plans to set a valuation range this week and begin trading on Thursday or Friday of next week, the Journal reported.
Investors will look to Anthropic’s valuation to gauge the strength of the AI boom. Some institutional investors are now pushing for a valuation below the $1.5 trillion target discussed as recently as last week, a figure that was itself considerably below the $2 trillion floated a few months ago, the report said.

Oops, something went wrong
This past week's stock market meltdown could hardly have come at a more critical moment for Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ). The sell-off cast a shadow over the frontier artificial intelligence developer's expected pre-Thanksgiving public debut, raising questions about its potential valuation and ability to sustain the next phase of AI growth.
"The only thing that matters the rest of this year is the Anthropic IPO," said Neostellar principal Willy Lee on Yahoo Finance's Market Hang. Lee said investors want to know whether Anthropic can sustain long-term growth and secure a meaningful share of the AI market.
"Those are the two questions that every investor is asking within their investment committee every single day before the IPO," said Lee.
Anthropic recently revealed revenue grew $1,206% to $33.2 billion through the first nine months of the year. The company also noted a staggering aggregate committed spend of $895.4 billion , which it says is primarily related to compute and infrastructure.
But the AI growth story was put to the test this past week as investors weighed a Democratic congressional win against the impact of the AI data center build-out. On Thursday, the Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) suffered its worst daily decline since April 2025, with chip stocks leading the declines.
The market turmoil prompted prospective buyers to discuss lowering Anthropic's valuation to a range of $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion, with some considering as low as $1.1 trillion, according to Bloomberg. That's far below estimates as high as $2 trillion projected in early October.
Amid increasingly jittery sentiment toward AI stocks, Anthropic faces a difficult decision, particularly if the unwinding of the AI trade continues.
"It would be difficult to go public," Anna Rathbun, founder and CEO of Grenadilla Advisory, told Yahoo Finance's Market Hang.
If Anthropic decides to delay its IPO, investors could interpret the move as a bearish signal for the AI trade, said Kevin Mahn, chief investment officer at Hennion & Walsh.
"If they don't delay, and their IPO fails, or comes in below expectations, that could be perceived as bearish to certain investors," said Mahn. "Damned if you do, damned if you don't."
Investors will also be looking for clues about the health of the AI trade on Nov. 17, when Nvidia ( NVDA ) reports earnings. With hyperscalers Alphabet ( GOOG , GOOGL ), Microsoft ( MSFT ), Amazon ( AMZN ), and Meta ( META ) having already reported, along with foundry Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing ( TSM ) and chip equipment maker ASML ( ASML ), expectations are high that Nvidia will once again beat earnings estimates and raise its guidance.
"We got so much confirmation already," said Shay Boloor, chief market strategist at Futurum. "I give it a 1% chance that they miss."

Asian technology stocks surged Tuesday, tracking a rebound on Wall Street overnight as a sharp decline in oil prices lifted sentiment while renewed buying in chip names spilled over into Asia, following last week's bruising sell-off.
Japan's technology investment giant SoftBank Group rose 13.88%, while chip-testing equipment maker Advantest gained 4.63%.
Semiconductor equipment maker Tokyo Electron rose over 6.05%, while Lasertec and Disco advanced 7.73% and 6.81%, respectively.
South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix jumped 6.69%, while Samsung Electronics rose 4.74%. Samsung SDI climbed 9.88%. Taiwan's TSMC added 2.24%.
China's tech-heavy ChiNext Price Index rose 1.46%.
The gains followed a strong session on Wall Street, where the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite climbed 2.74%, while the S&P 500 rose 2.35% to clock its best day since April 8.
The recovery came after a steep sell-off in global technology stocks last week, fueled by concerns that Democrats' sweeping victory in the U.S. midterm elections could lead to tighter restrictions on data-center development, potentially impacting demand for artificial intelligence chips and infrastructure.
"This is not to suggest that the tech sell-off is done and dusted. While there is some evidence that investors are taking advantage of last week's plunge to increase their exposure to chip and other AI-adjacent stocks, there's a danger that it may be a little bit premature to load up and 'buy the dip,'" said David Morrison, senior market analyst at Trade Nation.
Beyond the political uncertainty surrounding potential restrictions on data-center development, investors have also grown increasingly wary of the enormous capital expenditures required to build out AI infrastructure. Questions over how quickly those investments will translate into meaningful profits have weighed on sentiment toward companies across the semiconductor supply chain.

Federal regulators have launched a preliminary evaluation into more than 1.2 million Ford vehicles after side airbags deployed during crashes reportedly left multiple occupants with severe burns requiring medical treatment.

Some of the complaints received have reported injuries to law enforcement officers riding in Ford Explorer Police Interceptors.

articles.title_zh: Dow surges 1,100 points, Nasdaq climbs more than 2% as tech rebounds from last week’s tumult: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Stocks surged on Monday, boosted by a decline in oil prices as well as gains in technology shares after last week's volatility.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average popped 1,104.02 points, or 2.15%, to close at 52,389.75. The blue-chip index was supported by gains in stocks such as Goldman Sachs and Caterpillar . The S&P 500 rose 2.35% to end at 7,549.94 for its best day since April 8, while the Nasdaq Composite gained 2.74% to 25,253.14.
With Monday's rally, the Dow is now above the level it closed on Election Day. The S&P 500 and tech-heavy Nasdaq still remain slightly below, however.
Oil prices fell on Monday, lifting investor sentiment. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures dropped 4.38% to settle at $86.85 per barrel. International benchmark Brent slid 5.85% to $92.57 per barrel.
Friday's market partially rebounded from Thursday's brutal artificial intelligence-driven sell-off, as chip stocks recovered on renewed buying. However, concerns linger in the wake of the Democrats' strong midterm results, with investors fearing that tighter regulations on data center construction, energy use, and development costs could slow the AI infrastructure boom .
The tech sector also focused on the bombshell announcement Sunday that Nvidia's board of directors is opening an investigation into co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a businesswoman who U.S. intelligence agencies say is a Chinese spy. Nvidia shares closed down 4%.
"Magnificent Seven" names were higher contrary to Nvidia. Amazon gained about 3%, while Tesla and Alphabet climbed 5.5% and 1%, respectively. Microsoft also added almost 3%.
Other chip stocks advanced as well, with Broadcom popping nearly 9% and Advanced Micro Devices jumping 13%. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) — which dropped around 13% last week — rose more than 7%.
The recent chip sell-off was "overdone," said Jay Hatfield, CEO at Infrastructure Capital Advisors. The turmoil was still "partially correct," he added, given that there "definitely is a policy overhang from the Democrats in both the short run, but, more importantly, in the long run from '28." To be sure, he believes data centers are ultimately "going to get built" in the U.S.
For the broader market, Hatfield said that "it's not like the coast is clear" with Monday's bounce. In fact, he anticipates the S&P 500 will be rangebound through the end of the year.
"There are still a lot of overhangs on the market," the CEO said, pointing to elevated oil prices as a result of the Middle East conflict as well as the Federal Reserve's interest rate outlook.
This week , investors are looking ahead to key AI-related earnings — CoreWeave , Cisco and Applied Materials are all on deck — as they assess the outlook for tech and whether the recent sell-off has further to run.
They'll also watch for the releases of both the consumer price index on Tuesday and the producer price index on Friday, looking for clues on the Fed's next move.
The three U.S. leading indexes popped on Monday.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 1,104.02, or 2.15%, to settle at 52,389.75. The S&P 500 rose 2.35% to close at 7,549.94, while the Nasdaq Composite jumped 2.74% to 25,253.14.
The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) surged more than 8% to start the week amid a revival in tech shares.
Monday's advance in SOXX puts it on course for its best day since July 30.
Monolithic Power , a maker of power modules, and semiconductor giant Advanced Micro Devices were among the biggest advancers in the ETF, up 16% and 14%, respectively.
Nvidia was a standout underperformer, shedding more than 4%.
— Darla Mercado and Gina Francolla
S&P 500 energy was the only sector seeing losses in afternoon trading on Monday.
The group was last down 0.3%, adding to its one-week loss of more than 8%.
The remaining 10 S&P 500 sectors were in the green, led by industrials with a 4.2% gain. Consumer discretionary and information technology weren't too far behind, up 3.7% and 3%, respectively.
The S&P 500 was higher by more than 2% in afternoon trading Monday.
The move put the broad market index on pace for its best day since April 8, when it gained 2.51%.
— Nick Wells and Sean Conlon
General Motors' move to the Nasdaq on Nov. 17, and its possible inclusion in the Nasdaq-100 index as early as December, could bring increased investor visibility and focus to the overlooked automaker, according to Citi analyst Michael Ward.
If GM joins the Nasdaq-100 index it "would have a 0.2% weighting in the Index which represents about $4.6 billion of buying, or 10% of the non-indexed market cap," he wrote.
Additionally, he expects GM to buy back $10 billion in shares by the end of 2027, about 20% of the non-indexed market cap, which will support shares. If it joins, GM will become the cheapest stock in the index with the highest buyback yield, Ward noted.
CNBC recently said GM's switch to the Nasdaq could help it reframe its brand identity and boost its depressed valuation with the exposure to a new set of potential investors. Citi agreed.
"In our view, the structural improvements at GM and the North American industry have been missed, and if GM becomes part of the Nasdaq 100 Index, new investors will need to take a look which could bring added value to the stock," Ward wrote. The move helps reposition GM as a broad technology-first manufacturer, not just a combustion engine maker. "Consumer connection and complex manufacturing expertise position the auto sector to benefit from developing trends in energy storage, autonomous technologies, and connected platforms," wrote Ward.
Citi rates GM a buy with a $131 a share price target, which is more than 50% above Friday's close.

While stocks are bouncing back on Monday after last week's turbulence, they may not be over the hump yet.
"With many investors unwilling to stick their neck out right before year-end, we struggle to find many positive catalysts for stocks over the near-term," said Chris Senyek, the firm's chief investment strategist, in a Monday note.
Seeing downside risks, Senyek added, "We believe markets are likely to remain very news flow driven and need to hold critical technical support levels."
Currently, the S&P 500 is trading just above its 200-day moving average.

articles.title_zh: A short seller flagged Nvidia CEO's ties to a suspected Chinese spy six months before the scandal
articles.content_orig:
Six months before the Nvidia spy scandal emerged , the New York-based short seller firm Culper Research had already raised questions about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s unusually close relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that buys Nvidia chips. She is now suspected to be a Chinese spy.
The Nvidia CEO admitted to an extramarital affair over the weekend, and the company has now opened a formal investigation into his relationship with Alice Huang (who shares his last name but is not related). U.S. intelligence officials believe she was recruited by the Chinese government to collect intelligence on Jensen Huang and influence his position regarding U.S. export controls on advanced AI chips.
Culper’s May 13 report is resurfacing because it picked up on the connection between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang while investigating Megaspeed’s ties to Nvidia.
NEW: We are short Nvidia $NVDA . We believe Nvidia has a significant China problem. Please see our full report and disclosures now available on our website, link in bio. pic.twitter.com/oTaJyL7S2R
In particular, the report called the relationship between the two executives “uncomfortably close,” noting that the Nvidia CEO was spotted partying and socializing with Alice Huang on multiple occasions. The report even claimed that some Nvidia employees wondered whether they had a “special relationship.”
Culper Research also theorized the China business that Nvidia lost to export controls had been rerouted through Southeast Asia, and that Megaspeed, a major chip buyer in the region, was secretly financed by Chinese tech giant Alibaba through shell companies. It pointed to financial records that showed Megaspeed’s total liabilities and equity had grown from $33 million at the end of 2023 to around $3 billion by the end of 2024, much of it in the form of refundable deposits from an unidentified source.
Financial Times reported Monday that documents show Alibaba lent money to Megaspeed through subsidiaries.
Culper is a short seller, so it stood to financially benefit from making these allegations, and those about possible illegal chip diversion have not been independently verified. Its report is available on the web and was posted to X back in May .

articles.title_zh: Boeing to cut 5% of commercial jet workforce amid production struggles
articles.content_orig:
Boeing said Monday that it plans to cut 5% of its commercial airplane workforce as its production ramp-up is moving at a slower pace than the company expected.
The cuts will be through a combination of attrition and layoffs, Stephanie Pope, head of the commercial aircraft unit, said in a memo to staff.
Pope reiterated that the company is still working to stabilize production rates of its bestselling 737 Max planes, which are made outside of Seattle.
CEO Kelly Ortberg told investors last month that the company won't significantly increase production of the Max aircraft until the second half of next year. He said the company's wing production has been slower than expected.
"Adjusting our production schedules and reducing aircraft output puts us in an overstaffed position," Pope said in her note Monday. "Unfortunately, that means we need to align our staffing levels to our revised business plan, resulting in a reduction of approximately 5% through a combination of attrition and involuntary layoffs, with notifications beginning in December."
Boeing is targeting a production rate of 52 planes a month in the second half of 2027. Ortberg said the company has been trying to stabilize output at a rate of about 47 of its 737 Max planes a month.

articles.title_orig: Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond
articles.title_zh: Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond
articles.content_orig:
The tech world has spent the day digesting the extraordinary news that Jensen Huang - the charismatic, leather-jacket wearing chief executive of the multi-trillion dollar firm Nvidia - is being investigated by his own company over an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
None of us had that on our bingo cards for 2026.
Huang's alleged romantic affair with Alice Huang (no relation), the former CEO of a Singapore-based data centre company, has cast ripples far beyond his immediate family - undoubtedly on an emotional rollercoaster of their own - taking us to a crossroads at which technology, geopolitics and national security intersect.
In a nutshell, this is about the bitter rivalry between the US and China, as well as whether Jensen Huang has betrayed the US as well as his wife.
The US is locked in a fierce race with China to develop the best AI models.
"Whoever wins AI, wins," as US President Donald Trump puts it. He thinks that the country with the more dominant AI technology will benefit the most from it and, ultimately, will be the most powerful in the world. He may well be right.
Nvidia happens to make the best chips in the business for AI – so much so that it has been overwhelmed with demand.
It sets its prices accordingly: a single unit of the firm's latest kit for data centres starts at £37,000 ($50,000). A medium or large site might have hundreds of them.
The US administration initially slapped an export ban on Nvidia's more recent devices to prevent China from taking advantage of their superior capabilities. It has since softened the rules a little.
But there are suggestions that Alice Huang's company, Megaspeed, may have been involved in sneaking them into the country while she was in charge. Bloomberg reported that the firm bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia tech in November 2025. Megaspeed denies that it was used illegitimately.
For his part, Jensen Huang has lobbied heavily for the export rules between the two countries to be relaxed, arguing against the weight of general opinion that the AI race doesn't matter and that it would be no bad thing for China to become dependent on US tech.
"President Trump wants American to win and President Xi wants China to win, and it's possible for both of them to do so," he told the BBC last year.
It think it's safe to assume that neither country sees it that way.
The difficult questions Nvidia now has to try to answer include whether Alice gained special access to the firm's latest technology, either deliberately or not, via Jensen - and, if so, whether she shared it with Beijing or others.
We don't know when their affair began or ended , but there are numerous photos and videos of Jensen and Alice together at events. It is feasible that there were moments when they spent quite a lot of time together and Jensen has talked about always having an eye on his work.
China denies that she was engaged in espionage.
Interest in economic espionage is neither new nor unique to China. But many Western countries say that China does it on a grand scale, using a combination of technology tools and agents embedded in various organisations - including private companies.
China having access to significant enough numbers of Nvidia's chips to make use of them, or stripping them down and learning how to make its own versions, would infuriate the Trump administration, which is trying to keep its AI technology close to its chest.
Some models have even been withheld from the UK-based AI Safety Institute on the grounds that they are potentially too dangerous to be shared. The US does not want anyone having a headstart or misusing its innovations.
Another potential bombshell lies in the form of any national security information to which Jensen Huang may have been privy.
He is a man operating at the very top of the US elite - one of a handful of people who could probably walk into the White House unannounced and have tea with Trump. He has influence, he has access and he has powerful friends. It's quite possible that secrets were shared with him.
Nvidia says there's no evidence so far that he passed anything on and the firm has launched an internal investigation. Huang says he will co-operate and wants to keep his job - though if nothing else, he has broken Nvidia's own code of conduct, which states that company members should not have relationships with clients.
At present, he has the backing of both the Nvidia board and Trump, who described him as "honourable" and speculated that there must have been a reason for what had transpired. In other words, he's not throwing his tech boss buddy under the bus.
Nvidia's share price has fallen but has not tanked spectacularly, suggesting shareholders are not abandoning the company under his stewardship in their droves either.
An AI industry with a weakened Nvidia would undoubtedly be a slower one.
And there isn't really a natural successor waiting in the wings to replace Jensen were he forced out.
Huang has run Nvidia for more than 30 years - to many, he is Nvidia. He has steered it through multiple crises and it was his decision for the firm to focus on AI before it was trendy.
He is known to be a demanding boss who expects staff to work long hours and to high standards. There are stories about him calling all-staff meetings to tell off individuals who had made mistakes. He has said this was to prevent others making the same errors – but you can only imagine how it felt for those on the receiving end.
While he awaits the conclusion of the investigation into his actions, Huang must hope that, despite not tolerating the mistakes of his colleagues in the past, they will be gracious about his own failings.
And he must also live with the irony that he was potentially caught out not by a sophisticated high-tech sting, but by the oldest trick in the book: a honey trap.

articles.title_orig: A Sam Altman parody offers an amusing lesson in memory management
articles.title_zh: A Sam Altman parody offers an amusing lesson in memory management
articles.content_orig:
Sam Altman’s recent comments on the Cheeky Pint podcast inspired developer Iain Kay to create a satirical script that allows users to email the OpenAI CEO once per day if more than 10 percent of their system RAM is reported as available. Ram-Altman is described by its creator as a “parody project” launched in response to Altman’s viral remarks about RAM in your personal PC.
As reported by The Verge , on the October 29 episode recorded with Stripe President John Collison, Altman said, “A lot of people want local inference. And somehow, they assume that the problem is solved now because we are going to have open source models, we’re going to be able to run them on our computers, and so we’re not going to need all the stuff in the data center. But from a global allocation perspective, actually, it’s quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world’s limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used 5 percent of the time.”
Altman has since explained that his comments were taken out of context and briefly changed his display name to “RAM Altman” on X, which Kay calls on the project GitHub, “objectively excellent and where the project gets its name.”
In an email to Ars, Kay said, “Ram-Altman is a bash script that takes MemTotal minus MemAvailable from /proc/meminfo, so the figure includes page cache and reclaimable slab but leaves out tmpfs and shared memory.”
If the script only showed what Linux reports as “free” RAM, it would paint an incomplete picture. Linux often reports a surprisingly small amount of “free” RAM, as it doesn’t count memory that is currently claimable for use. Linux will fill available RAM caches with file data for quick access, but the kernel can reclaim that usage at a moment’s notice when needed. The MemAvailable figure is the kernel’s own estimate of how much memory it could hand over without swapping.
Users can schedule the script to ask the kernel for a status update every five minutes, and if more than 10 percent of RAM is available, it triggers a joke email from one of several joke templates. The script limits outgoing emails to one per day.
The GitHub page for the RAM-Altman project includes a dry-run option that any Linux user with a Bash terminal should be able to paste and run without the need for email trolling. When the threshold is exceeded, each dry run output features one generated joke email, so repeated runs produce different amusing examples.
A test run of the script on my Fedora 44 KDE machine confirmed the author’s measurements. Inside the System – Info Center of my Fedora desktop, the system reports 14.9 GiB of total usable system RAM after the kernel and firmware take their needed slices of the 16 GiB of physical memory. This reflects the total amount of capacity the system has to work with, not the amount available at any given time. The Ram-Altman script shows that of that 14.9 GiB total pool, 10 GiB is used, with 4.9 GiB available (33.1 percent). That figure isn’t the simple sum of the “free” and “cache” lines that the script displays, but a kernel-calculated figure that accounts for the full amount of memory that can be reclaimed.
The project concedes the nuance that Altman was referring to how much time memory spends being utilized, while the script measures how much capacity is free at the time of measurement. While the script might tell Altman that 33 percent of your system RAM is available, it doesn’t outline how often that’s the case. The concession steps on the joke slightly, but it keeps everyone honest.
The GitHub is wise to point out that “ --dry-run is the best way to enjoy this. It costs nothing and all the jokes are there.” Used irresponsibly, this cheeky joke could morph into a harassment tool, and Kay quickly points out that the script does not include anyone’s email, including Altman’s. Users who deploy their own operating version are encouraged to only use their own real email addresses and honor any requests to stop, as is outlined at the bottom of the script-generated output.
If you’re interested in taking a look at some of the emails generated without having to spin up a Linux machine that reports the system status every five minutes, the ram-altman.lol project website rotates through sample emails generated by the script. Kay writes on the website that, “In fairness, he says the remarks were taken out of context , posted ‘i want you to have so much ram’ , and briefly went by Ram Altman on X. That makes this script a daily progress report.”
